entry.title: Exploring SAP BTP - A Cybersecurity Student's Perspective on Building Secure Enterprise Applications
entry.content:
Introduction

As a Cybersecurity student, studying Artificial Intelligence and Cybersecurity at the same time, my studies have so far revolved around the here and now. My colleagues and I discuss network security, delve into the details of various malicious software, engage in penetration testing scenarios, and analyze the aftermath. We study bits, scan ports, capture packets, and set up intrusion detection systems. Cybersecurity is a dynamic and diverse field that offers plenty of specializations, each with technical challenges to be solved. At the same time, there is always room for further improvement and development. While the technical aspects of cyber defense are usually found in the network infrastructure, I felt that there were also essential security concepts to be learned elsewhere.


Outside of the university network, beyond the local infrastructure, there are enterprise applications. They comprise their own set of security solutions, procedures, and rules. I was interested to learn how such software handles the challenges that a typical enterprise faces on a daily basis. How does an organization that employs thousands of individuals across continents and time zones manage to grant access to corporate databases to every single authorized employee? How are permissions structured so that every individual can perform only their required tasks and nothing more? How do API interfaces protect themselves against unauthorized access while sharing data with external partners and clients? How does the enterprise ensure that nothing suspicious takes place within the application programming interfaces and data structures while maintaining acceptable performance standards for thousands of users? How do cloud-based applications communicate with older on-premises enterprise resource planning software?


By asking these questions, I uncovered the SAP Business Technology Platform, a comprehensive ecosystem that secures its modern cloud-based enterprise software extensions. SAP is the software giant at the center of the world’s exchange of goods and services. It is hard to overestimate the scale of SAP’s impact on the world economy and how critical it is for the proper functioning of enterprises worldwide. Therefore, learning about SAP’s security solutions is the ultimate enterprise-level cybersecurity lesson. The present article summarizes my findings and the general understanding of SAP BTP’s approach to cybersecurity.

 

What is SAP BTP?

SAP BTP is not a cloud hosting platform as one might imagine at first glance. It does not merely provide virtual machines via the cloud; instead, it offers software products that extend, implement, and integrate enterprise-class apps. On this platform, companies can build business apps, automate processes, leverage artificial intelligence, analyze big data, and integrate systems.


Since SAP BTP provides the bridge over which the ERP databases, customer platforms, and external APIs, are interconnected, it is a privileged guardian of the data that passes through. Critical financial information, personal employee data, and customer records are constantly processed within the services. For this reason, the security of this platform is of paramount importance since the vital data of the enterprise is deeply involved in the functioning of the applications. One should be aware that the security of these services is what protects the digital core of a company; therefore, weaknesses in their protection can damage the reputation of a global enterprise.

 

Why Enterprise Security is Different

Enterprise applications are high-value targets. A successful attack could lead to a damaged web page, but more severely, it could lead to the loss of millions of dollars, the theft of intellectual property, or even regulatory penalties. Attackers continue to target enterprise applications through sophisticated means, such as stealing user credentials, privilege escalation, session hijacking, application programming interface (API) abuse, insider threats, data exfiltration, supply chain attacks, and cloud misconfigurations.


The key differentiator is the blast radius - if one account is compromised, and it has access to many other resources, a major breach can occur. Attackers can laterally move from one compromised system to another connected system through available links, such as active directory connections, and gain access to critical enterprise systems such as the enterprise resource planning (ERP) database and make unauthorized changes to the database, for example, payroll manipulation. One compromised account can affect an enterprise as a whole. A comprehensive defense-in-depth approach to securing enterprise applications should be implemented by enforcing security at all levels instead of relying on one primary security solution, such as firewalls, and shifting the focus to identity governance.

 

Identity Authentication

Identity is the new perimeter. We do not have the luxury of corporate firewalls in the cloud anymore, as users are no longer connecting to the system from a corporate network but from different devices and locations. As such, authentication is the first security layer, and it should be strong to withstand brute-force attacks. In SAP BTP, this security aspect is managed by the Identity Authentication Service (IAS).
IAS’s main functions are to provide identity authentication with increased security levels. The service allows organizations to establish a centralized Single Sign-On (SSO), enforce complex password policies, and enable multi-factor authentication. Using IAS also ensures the possibility to federate identities and connect the SAP BTP applications to the corporate user database. The benefit of such an approach is that it minimizes the attack surface, thereby reducing the risks significantly. Additionally, the users have one set of credentials, which increases convenience, and a centralized identity database makes the management easier and more secure, as there is no need to remember multiple passwords. Finally, if a company decides to terminate the employment of a database of an employee, all applications connected to IAS will automatically block the access of this person.

 

Authorization Collections & RBAC

Whereas authentication is about “Who are you?”, authorization is about “What are you allowed to do?”. SAP BTP implements the concept of authorization using the Role-Based Access Control where the users are only granted access to resources according to their roles. The system uses the Authorization Collections to manage access, which in turn consists of RBAC roles. In other words, the permissions (scopes) are grouped into roles, and these roles are further organized into role collections.


Such an approach follows the Least Privilege and Separation of Duties principles. The former implies that users are only given the minimum required to perform their tasks, while the latter ensures that one set of duties cannot be performed by just a single person. For instance, in the finance department, the employees should not be able to modify the HR information, whereas developers should not have access to payroll data. In case one of these users has their credentials compromised, the breach would only be limited to the functions of the particular exploited account.

 

Secure APIs and OAuth

Modern applications tend to use various APIs to provide their data. However, there are some security risks, such as passwords embedded in code, exposure of API keys, and stolen credentials. The OAuth 2.0 protocol is one of the security standards used by the SAP BTP to establish secure communication between API clients and servers.
The OAuth protocol allows making the API more secure by replacing user credentials with short-lived access tokens. These tokens are issued upon presenting client credentials and have a limited scope and lifetime. Such a mechanism ensures that even if an unauthorized third party gains access to a token, they would not be able to use it for long and for malicious purposes. Overall, the OAuth protocol is a robust and standardized way to secure communication between systems in the enterprise application environment.

 

Encryption

 

Data protection involves encryption. SAP BTP ensures the data encryption in transit as well as at rest to ensure the safety of the transferred information and data at rest. First, data encryption in transit is used during the data transmission process and is provided by the HTTPS protocol and Transport Layer Security (TLS 1.2 or TLS 1.3). Second, data encryption at rest involves the use of encryption algorithms during the storage of data on physical devices. SAP BTP databases, including SAP HANA Cloud, protect the data volumes, backups, and logs with AES-256 encryption algorithms. In addition, the software uses certificates and encryption key management to ensure the regular rotation of keys and protect data from being extracted from physical media or unauthorized access from outside.

 

Monitoring and Audit Logs

Security includes not only the prevention of unwanted events but also the ability to respond by providing visibility into what has occurred. To ensure this visibility, organizations need to capture and maintain logs that document relevant security events for meeting compliance requirements and enabling security investigations. The SAP audit log service provides this type of security and compliance visibility by capturing and storing detailed information about relevant events, such as user authentication attempts, configuration changes, and other relevant activities specific to the SAP Business Technology Platform.


These logs are always tamper-proof and in a read-only format and can be used to meet various compliance-related needs. Additionally, by being able to forward such logs to a centralized log management solution, such as a Security Information and Event Manager (SIEM) solution, SOC analysts can monitor and detect potential malicious activities in near-real-time and take immediate action to ensure business operations’ integrity.

 

Security Best Practices I Learned

My analysis of SAP BTP revealed a number of relevant security measures, which can be directly applied to general cybersecurity practices, as well as their specific enterprise-level implementation. The table below demonstrates the correlation between the two.

 

Practice

Why it Matters

Example

MFA

Stops stolen passwords from granting access.

Enforce MFA on all SAP Cloud Identity Services login screens.

Least Privilege

Limits attacker movement in case of compromise.

Assign specific Role Collections to business users rather than admin roles.

Logging

Helps investigations and forensic auditing.

Enable the SAP Audit Log service and forward logs to a SIEM.

Encryption

Protects sensitive data from intercept or physical theft.

Configure TLS 1.3 for network connections and AES-256 at rest.

OAuth

Provides safer APIs and secure system integrations.

Generate short-lived JWT tokens for system-to-system interfaces.

RBAC

Enforces controlled access based on job function.

Separate billing, development, and system administration permissions.

Regular Reviews

Removes unnecessary permissions over time.

Perform quarterly audits of active role assignments and group members.

 

Cybersecurity Perspective

Coming from penetration testing and cybersecurity, you, by default, tend to see weaknesses. When you work in a lab environment, you naturally ask yourself, ‘how do I exploit this?’ or ‘how do I bypass this firewall?’ When you look at SAP BTP, it is not the weaknesses you first notice, rather it is the strength, and you begin to wonder how to apply these ideas elsewhere: ‘How would a secure enterprise system be built from the ground up?’ This is an incredibly powerful shift in perspective, and it is useful for all those looking to develop strong, secure cloud-based software in the future.
This change in thinking helps you move from a mindset of exploiting weakness to a mindset of designing security into an application from the start. These are both incredibly important skills, but the latter clearly has far wider application, as it helps you build secure systems that keep working even if one element is compromised.

 

Future Areas I Want to Explore

My research so far has only touched on the periphery of enterprise security. In the future, I would like to investigate the following areas:
SAP Build Apps to research how the security policies are implemented in the low-code development environment. I would like to take a closer look at the Integration Suite to understand how secure application programming interfaces (APIs) and data integration are, and investigate SAP Cloud Identity Services to learn more about advanced access control and governance in the cloud environment. Moreover, I would like to learn more about securing databases in the context of SAP HANA Cloud and artificial intelligence (AI) security in the SAP AI Core environment and implement automated testing and scanning in the DevSecOps pipeline to ensure that security requirements are met.

 

And now let's hear from you!

What do you imagine or predict is the future of AI and Cybersecurity — and how are you preparing for it?

Drop your thoughts in the comments below — I'd love to hear where you think the field is heading! 🚀

Dino C D | MSc AI & Cybersecurity Student, Christ University, Bengaluru

entry.title: Beyond Role-Based Access: Authorization Policies in SAP Risk and Assurance Management
entry.content:
Managing who sees what in a compliance system sounds straightforward – until your organization spans multiple regions, business units, and regulatory frameworks. A role assignment that grants access to all objects (such as all issues or risks) can quickly become a liability.

 

The Limitation of Roles Alone

SAP Risk and Assurance Management (RAM) ships with a robust role-based model. Assign a user the Compliance Specialist role, and they can work with issues across the board. For organizations where a SOX team should never see tax-related issues, or where risk managers in one entity have no business viewing another's data, this falls short.

 

A More Granular Option

Authorization Policies offer a policy-based alternative for three services: GRC Issue Management, GRC Risk, and GRC Control. Instead of asking only "what can this user do?", policies also ask "on which data?". A specialist handling indirect taxes sees only those issues. A risk manager scoped to one organizational unit works only within that boundary.

Policies are maintained in SAP Cloud Identity Services and assigned to individual users – not groups.

 

Mixing Models – With One Important Caveat

The two models can coexist in four ways: policies for all supported services, policies for selected services only, policies for selected users while others stay role-based, or roles only. This flexibility makes phased adoption practical.

The caveat: when both a role and a policy are assigned to the same user for the same service, the role authorizations override the policy restrictions. Predefined role collections must be removed from policy-managed users to ensure data restrictions actually take effect.

 

Reference

For full  setup guidance, see https://help.sap.com/docs/risk-and-assurance-management/admin-guide-risk-and-assurance-management/authorization-management in SAP Risk and Assurance Management Administration Guide.

entry.title: Access Provisioning in SAP BTP Using SAP GRC Access Control 12.0
entry.content:
1. Introduction

SAP GRC Access Control is commonly used to govern access requests, approvals, risk analysis, provisioning, and audit trails for SAP systems. Standard provisioning connectors cover many traditional target systems, but SAP BTP role collection provisioning is not available as a standard connector in SAP GRC landscape.

This blog explains how SAP GRC Access Control (AC) can be extended to provision and deprovision SAP BTP role collections through XSUAA APIs while still using the standard MSMP workflow, provisioning engine, and GRC audit log framework.

2. Business Requirement

The requirement was to submit SAP BTP access requests from SAP GRC AC, route them through the normal MSMP approval path, and automatically provision the approved BTP role collection to the user in XSUAA. 

This requirement commonly appears in a hybrid landscape where organizations use S/4 HANA On-Premise or Private Cloud Edition together with BTP Build Work Zone for the Fiori Launchpad. In this model, backend authorizations are managed in the S/4 HANA ABAP system, while Fiori Launchpad view access is managed in BTP. Roles from both systems can be combined into a single business role and provisioned together.

3. High-Level Architecture

The solution uses the standard GRC adapter dispatch mechanism. A custom connector type is configured in GRC, and the provisioning framework dispatches approved requests to a custom ABAP adapter that implements IF_GRAC_AD_ACCESS_MGMT.

4. Generating the Client Key and Secret in SAP BTP

The ABAP adapter needs an OAuth client that can call the required XSUAA and authorization management APIs. In this proof of concept, the client key and secret were generated from SAP BTP. The exact service plan, scopes, and authorizations may vary by subaccount and security policy.

I used the SAP BTP CLI to generate the client key and secret. The same setup can also be performed from SAP BTP cockpit, depending on the tenant and authorizations available. You can follow the SAP tutorial at Get Started with the SAP BTP Command Line Interface (btp CLI) to enable BTP CLI on your local machine.

Run the following commands from PowerShell on Windows or Terminal on macOS:

btp target --subaccount <Subaccount ID>
btp create security/api-credential --name <unique api name>

Save the returned values securely in JSON format. These values are used by the ABAP HTTP client or, preferably, by an OAuth configuration maintained in the ABAP stack.

{
  "clientid": "<Client id based on API name like api!b12345>",
  "clientsecret": "<generated-secret>",
  "url": "https://<subdomain>.authentication.<region>.hana.ondemand.com",
  "apiurl": "api.authentication.<region>.hana.ondemand.com"
}

 

5. Creating Connector in SM59

For the BTP provisioning integration, RFC HTTP destinations are required so the custom GRC adapter can call SAP BTP/XSUAA REST API endpoints from the ABAP stack. The destinations should be created as type G: HTTP Connection to External Server, and the security settings should be aligned with the OAuth design used in your landscape.

6. Custom ABAP Adapter Implementation

7. XSUAA API Calls Used by the Adapter

The custom client class ZCL_BTP_XSUAA_CLIENT wraps the XSUAA and SCIM API calls. The key operations are token retrieval, user lookup, role collection lookup, assignment, removal, and optional user creation/deletion.

7.1 OAuth Token

Authorization: Basic <base64(clientid:clientsecret)>

grant_type=client_credentials

  "access_token": "eyJhbGciOiJSUzI1NiIs...",
  "token_type": "bearer",
  "expires_in": 43199
}

7.2 Find User

Authorization: Bearer <access_token>
Accept: application/scim+json

{
  "Resources": [
    {
      "id": "8f5c2d10-....",
      "userName": "TEST_BTP",
      "origin": "sap.default"
    }
  ],
  "totalResults": 1
}

7.3 Create User

POST /Users
Authorization: Bearer <access_token>
Content-Type: application/scim+json

{
  "userName": "TEST_BTP",
  "origin": "sap.default",
  "name": {
    "givenName": "Test",
    "familyName": "User"
  },
  "emails": [
    { "value": "TEST_BTP@test.com", "primary": true }
  ],
  "active": true
}

7.4 Find Role Collection / Group

GET /Groups?filter=displayName eq "AI_UseCase_GeneralUser"
Authorization: Bearer <access_token>
Accept: application/scim+json

7.5 Assign Role Collection

PATCH /Groups/<group-id>
Authorization: Bearer <access_token>
Content-Type: application/scim+json

{
  "schemas": [
    "urn:ietf:params:scim:api:messages:2.0:PatchOp"
  ],
  "Operations": [
    {
      "op": "add",
      "path": "members",
      "value": [
        {
          "value": "8f5c2d10-....",
          "display": "TEST_BTP"
        }
      ]
    }
  ]
}

7.6 Remove Role Collection

PATCH /Groups/<group-id>
Authorization: Bearer <access_token>
Content-Type: application/scim+json

{
  "schemas": [
    "urn:ietf:params:scim:api:messages:2.0:PatchOp"
  ],
  "Operations": [
    {
      "op": "remove",
      "path": "members[value eq \"8f5c2d10-....\"]"
    }
  ]
}

7.7 Delete User

DELETE /Users/<user-id>
Authorization: Bearer <access_token>

 

8. Connector Configuration in SPRO

The connector configuration follows the standard GRC connector setup steps used for other target applications.

       A. Maintain Connectors and Connection Types

  1. Create custom connection type ZBTP
  2. Define connector as shown in the screenshot
  3. Assign connector to connector group

       B. Maintain Connection Settings

  1. Add a new scenario for ZBTP and assign class/interface ZCL_GRAC_AD_ACCESS_MGMT_BTP for provisioning.

  2. Similarly, assign ZCL_GRAC_AD_AUTH_MGMT_BTP to the AUTH and ROLMG scenarios for repository and authorization related operations.
  3. Subsequently, add the BTP target connector for each of these scenarios.

       C. Maintain Connector Settings

Maintain the required connector parameters for the custom BTP connector.

    

       D. Maintain Mapping for Actions and Connector Groups

  1. Maintain new connector group BTP



  2. Assign actions to the connector group for the BTP API connector

 

9. Repository Object Sync

Select the BTP API connector and run a full repository object synchronization job. This brings the BTP role collections and users into GRC tables (GRACRLCONN and GRACUSERCONN).

 

10. Access Provisioning

After the access request is submitted and approved, the GRC AC provisioning audit log shows the requested role collection assignment after the adapter returns the operation result to the standard provisioning framework.

The SAP BTP subaccount audit log also records the role collection assignment, providing confirmation from the target platform.

Note: The audit logs of SAP GRC and BTP may show different timestamps depending on the SAP system timezone setting and the browser time zone.

11. Security and Credential Handling

For a proof of concept, the client key and secret can be read by the custom ABAP client during token retrieval. For production, credentials should be managed through approved SAP mechanisms such as OAuth 2.0 client configuration, secure storage, and restricted authorization to the relevant SM59 destinations.

The OAuth client should be scoped only for the required XSUAA and SCIM operations, and the integration user should not receive broader administrative permissions than needed. Network access, TLS validation, audit logging, and credential rotation should be reviewed with the security team before production rollout.

Disclaimer:
This blog describes a proof of concept implementation. Security requirements, network controls, credential handling, audit expectations, and compliance obligations vary from organization to organization. Before implementing this solution in a productive landscape, review it with your security, Basis, network, audit, and SAP platform teams. Consider stronger patterns such as mTLS, SAP Integration Suite, SAP Cloud Connector based broker services, private connectivity, or organization-approved secret management wherever required.

 

12. Conclusion

This integration shows that SAP GRC Access Control can remain the central governance and approval layer even when the target access is in SAP BTP. By using the standard MSMP workflow and provisioning framework, users can request BTP role collections through the same controlled process used for other enterprise systems.

The key design point is the custom connector adapter. Instead of bypassing GRC, the adapter translates approved GRC provisioning actions into XSUAA and SCIM API calls for user lookup, role collection assignment, removal, and audit feedback. This keeps the access request, approval, provisioning status, and audit trail visible in GRC while extending the reach of the platform to cloud-native access.

For production use, the implementation should be hardened with secure OAuth credential handling, least-privilege scopes, proper destination configuration, monitoring, and operational error handling. With those controls in place, this approach can provide a practical bridge between SAP GRC AC and SAP BTP role collection governance.

 

13. References

  1. https://developers.sap.com/tutorials/cp-sapcp-getstarted.html
  2. https://api.sap.com/api/PlatformAPI/overview

 

Thanks,
Mukesh

entry.title: Cyber Resilience Act: What It Means for SAP and Our Customers
entry.content:
Cybersecurity is becoming one of the defining factors in how digital products are designed, developed, and maintained. The EU Cyber Resilience Act (CRA) represents a significant milestone in establishing comprehensive cybersecurity requirements for digital products, and SAP is fully committed to meeting these standards.

In my role as Communications Lead for SAP’s Cyber Resilience Act (CRA) program, I collaborate with teams across security, compliance, and product areas to help drive awareness and communication around SAP’s CRA initiatives and priorities.

SAP, the CRA regulatory requirements reflect the importance we place on building robust and trustworthy security foundations that support businesses worldwide.

The regulation entered into force in December 2024, with most obligations expected to apply from December 2027. It introduces cybersecurity expectations for products with digital elements throughout their lifecycle—from design and development to maintenance and vulnerability management.

 

What is the Cyber Resilience Act?
The Cyber Resilience Act establishes common cybersecurity requirements for hardware and software products with digital elements across the European Union.

It aims to strengthen trust in digital products by addressing two important aspects:

  • Improving cybersecurity levels in digital products by reducing vulnerabilities and ensuring consistent security updates
  • Empowering users with clearer information and greater awareness, enabling them to make confident, well-informed security decisions when selecting and using digital solutions

To advance these objectives, the CRA requires organizations to:

  • Embed security considerations early in product development
  • Strengthen vulnerability and incident reporting and response processes
  • Provide security updates to address vulnerabilities and ensure the continued security of products whenever necessary
  • Demonstrate compliance through CE marking
  • Maintain security-related documentation across the product lifecycle

The regulation applies to virtually all connected products, from IoT devices to enterprise software, with fines up to €15 million or 2.5% of global annual turnover for non compliance.

 

SAP’s CRA Journey
Our Commitment
Security has long been an integral part of how SAP builds and delivers products. The CRA aligns with many of the principles that already guide our development practices. 

As highlighted during SAP’s Cyber Security Month, security is not only about technology—it is also about our people, and how our teams build, secure, and support our products. 

Preparing for CRA readiness is therefore not simply about meeting regulatory expectations. It is about SAP’s commitment to security and resilience to strengthen the trust customers place in SAP solutions.

Our Progress So Far
To support CRA readiness across our portfolio, SAP has established a dedicated program bringing together experts from multiple areas, including:

  • Product development
  • Security engineering
  • Compliance and legal teams

Some of the key activities underway include:

  • Assessing current security practices against CRA expectations
  • Enhancing vulnerability management and response processes
  • Integrating security considerations more deeply into development lifecycles

 

What This Means for SAP Customers
Stronger Security Foundations
Security considerations are increasingly embedded throughout the product lifecycle—from
design to operation.

Improved Vulnerability Handling
Enhanced processes help ensure that vulnerabilities can be identified, assessed, and
addressed efficiently.

Greater Transparency
Customers gain improved visibility into security practices, documentation, and incident
communication.

Regulatory Alignment
SAP solutions offered in the EU markets align with the CRA cybersecurity expectations.

 

Key Focus Areas
Security Throughout the Development Process

  • Integrating security considerations early in product design 
  • Expanding threat modeling and risk assessment practices
  • Increasing automation in security testing across development pipelines

Vulnerability Management

  • Improving workflows for vulnerability identification and assessment 
  • Strengthening coordinated disclosure with security researchers
  • Enhancing patch development and deployment capabilities

Incident Response

  • Maintaining monitoring and response capabilities
  • Aligning processes with European reporting frameworks
  • Supporting clear and timely customer communication during incidents

Documentation and Transparency

  • Providing structured security documentation for products
  • Supporting compliance reporting to market surveillance authorities
  • Ensuring customers have access to relevant security information

What do you see as the biggest challenge in preparing for CRA requirements?
The biggest challenge is integrating security, engineering, and compliance across the entire lifecycle and under one system to manage compliance more effectively. While SAP does meet specific individual requirements, aligning these cohesively will create an organizational shift beneficial towards completing the CRA readiness picture. We invite you to join us on this journey and contribute to making the digital world safer for everyone.

 

The Role of the SAP Community
The Cyber Resilience Act will shape how digital products are built and maintained in the coming years. Security is strongest when it is built collaboratively, and the SAP Community plays a vital role in strengthening the overall security ecosystem — contributing valuable insights that help improve security practices across organizations.

We invite you to stay connected and take part in the discussion:

  • Join the Security and Compliance Community to stay connected and participate in discussions around cybersecurity, compliance, and cyber resilience. 
  • Attend community sessions to explore best practices and emerging topics — including the monthly SAP Security Webcast series highlighting topics relevant to SAP customers. 
  • Share your implementation experiences, insights, and best practices with fellow community members in the Security and Compliance community. Use tags such as #CyberResilienceAct #CRA #SAP #Cybersecurity #Compliance #ProductSecurity #SecurityByDesign #VulnerabilityManagement #SecurityCompliance to help your post reach the right audience. 
  • Contribute to a stronger security ecosystem through responsible vulnerability disclosure and collaborative knowledge sharing

How is your organization preparing for the Cyber Resilience Act? Are there specific security practices or challenges you are already addressing?
In case you have questions to SAP, please contact your SAP account representative. SAP is committed to cybersecurity excellence. Together with our community, we're building a more secure digital future where businesses can innovate with confidence, knowing their systems are protected by the highest security standards.

CRA SharePoint (under construction) | SAP Global Security & Cloud compliance | Security and Compliance Community | #CyberResilienceAct #CRA #SAP #Cybersecurity #Compliance #ProductSecurity #SecurityByDesign #VulnerabilityManagement
#SecurityCompliance

 

Looking Ahead
Over the coming years, SAP will continue strengthening its security posture while preparing for CRA readiness.

Our focus includes:

  • Completing product assessments across the SAP portfolio
  • Expanding security testing within development processes
  • Enhancing transparency and communication around security capabilities
  • Collaborating with regulators and industry partners

Beyond regulatory alignment, SAP remains committed to advancing security innovation and supporting a safer digital environment for customers and partners worldwide.
