entry.title: Importance of Defining Agency and Accountability Before Deploying AI Agents
entry.content:
Premise:

Every CIO that I am speaking to is exploring the deployment of AI agents within their organizations, in ways that make business sense. The primary thinking is from an RoI perspective, will it save us more than it will cost us. And a lot of them still struggle in finding the right business problem to be solved using these agents. And almost every one of the CIO’s that I am talking to is also exploring working with multiple AI agent providers to avoid lock in.

I have realized that among all the discussions and decisions that are happening around deploying agents, one key question remains usually unanswered – How will the agents be governed and who will be accountable for the actions of each one of these agents.

The dichotomy here is that for all the low stake situations where this question may not matter much are also the same situations where they can’t really find substantial value. And for every situation where there is substantial value to be reaped, the question of accountability becomes even more important.

The honest answer to this question on accountability is uncomfortable – every leader in your organization is accountable.

Not the model vendor. Not the system integrator. Not the AI platform provider. The enterprise that chose to deploy the agent, configure its permissions, and send it to work inside live business processes carries the accountability. Full stop. That is the legal position, it is increasingly the regulatory position, and it is the operational reality that CIOs are now navigating in real time.

The Cloud Security Alliance's research note on AI liability puts it plainly: deploying an AI agent does not transfer liability to the agent — it concentrates accountability on the deploying organisation, under an emerging "reasonable oversight" standard.

Enterprises are liable unless they can demonstrate that monitoring, audit trails, and safety controls were in place “before” any negative incident happens.

The problem is that most enterprises are not deploying with that standard in mind. They are deploying with speed or Return on investment in mind.

The Numbers Are Stark

According to Gravitee's State of AI Agent Security report, 81% of enterprise teams are planning to deploy more AI agents in the next 12 months. And around 85% have no formal accountability structure for an AI Agent behavior. More troubling is that 54% of organisations report confirmed security incidents in the past year. And only 19.7% say all of their agents are fully secured and governed before going live. 

The root cause of most of these incidents, Gravitee found, is not a rogue model or an adversarial prompt. It is missing governance — absent identity controls, unclear permission boundaries, no documented process to pause or revoke access, and no named person accountable for agent behaviour.

Meanwhile, on the CIO side of the equation, IBM's Institute for Business Value survey of 2,000 technology executives found that two-thirds of CIOs and CTOs are accountable for AI systems they do not fully control, because agents are being spun up by business units, vendors, and partners well outside the CIO's direct visibility. 

Accountability without authority. Responsibility without visibility. This is the governance crisis hiding inside the AI deployment boom waiting to blow up in our faces.

Why This Is Different From Previous Technology Waves

The governance challenge with AI agents is structurally different from anything we have dealt with before in enterprise technology. When we deployed ERP systems, the system did what it was programmed to do. Variance was a bug. When we deployed RPA bots, they were brittle but deterministic, you could read the script. When we deployed predictive analytics, humans still made the final call on the recommendation.

AI agents are different. They plan, reason and take sequential actions across systems, reading data, calling APIs, executing transactions and sometimes without human oversight. More importantly, they can be wrong in ways that we can not predict in advance.

Traditional governance assumed that a human made any and all consequential decisions. That assumption is now broken.

SAP's architecture team frames this well. They state that in an AI-native enterprise, agents operate as first-class enterprise principals, they authenticate, receive authorizations, and are governed like any other enterprise actor. But unlike a human employee, their behavior at scale cannot be supervised one decision at a time. 

The governance response, therefore, cannot be a policy document or a post-deployment audit. It has to be engineering and done at the time of designing the system and inbuilt into the architecture, before the agent goes anywhere near a production system or makes any decision.

The Accountability Gap Is a Design Flaw, Not an Oversight

Here is the reframe I want to offer - when an enterprise deploys AI agents without governance built in, the accountability gap that results is not an oversight, it is a design flaw. And like any design flaw, the cost of fixing it grows exponentially over time. The later in the lifecycle you catch it, the more expensive it is to fix. The amount of damage that can result if an agent ends up acting in ways that are harmful, either to the organization or our stakeholders can potentially be catastrophic. 

SAP's recent blog post, "Who Controls the Controller?", captures this precisely. It argues that governance of agentic AI is a GRC imperative, not a technology question.

It also argues that before deploying agents at scale, leaders must answer these questions clearly and unambiguously, and for each agent being deployed:

  • Which decisions the agent can make autonomously
  • Which decisions require human approval (human-in-the-loop)
  • How agent behaviour is monitored in production
  • Who is accountable if the agent causes harm

This accountability needs to be embedded in the roles and responsibilities of the identified person and not just mentioned in passing as an afterthought.

And then the post lands the line that I think every CIO and CDO needs to hear: "AI made the decision" is no longer a valid defence. The CFO, CCO, CRO, and board cannot outsource this to the model. It comes back to the enterprise. Which means it comes back to you.

You should not only be able to clearly identify who was accountable for an issue when it happens but also be able to trace the reason why the issue happened. This traceability becomes crucial in order to address any issues that are found in the agent’s behavior or decision-making ability.

What "Accountability by Design" Actually Looks Like

I am not advocating for governance theatre - compliance checklists that satisfy an audit and do nothing to reduce real risk. I am talking about five practical design disciplines that need to be non-negotiable before any AI agent goes live in a business-critical context. 

1. Agent Identity Before Anything Else

Every agent that touches your enterprise systems needs a verifiable identity. Not a shared service account. Not a hardcoded API key. A real, scoped identity with its own authentication credentials, authorisation boundaries, and audit trail. Gravitee's research identifies reliance on shared credentials as the single most common structural vulnerability in enterprise AI deployments — they call it the "new shadow IT."

AI Agents should be treated exactly as you would treat a new employee - onboarded formally, given the minimum permissions needed to do the job, and de-provisioned when the job is done.

2. Scoped Permissions, Not Broad Access

AI Agents that can access everything are a liability, not an asset. SAP's AI-native architecture is explicit on this. Agents should operate with bounded authorizations, and users should only be able to delegate a subset of their own permissions for unattended execution. The principle of least privilege applies to AI agents at least as much as it applies to human users. 

3. Human-in-the-Loop for High-Stakes Decisions

Not every agent decision needs a human. Most should not. That would defeat the purpose. But the threshold for human approval needs to be defined in advance, not negotiated after an incident. Following questions need to be answered in advance:

  • What are your high-risk transaction types?
  • What is the monetary threshold above which an agent must pause and escalate?
  • Which data classes should never be touched without human confirmation?

These are business judgements, not technical configurations, and they need to be made by your executive team, not your IT architects, and done so before go-live.

4. A Governed Control Plane, Not a De-centralised Fleet

One of the most dangerous patterns I see is what I call the "agent sprawl" problem. Teams across the business deploying their own agents, using different models, different tools, different permission schemes, with no central visibility. This is the new version of shadow IT.

You cannot govern what you cannot see. SAP AI Agent Hub was built to address exactly this. It is a vendor-agnostic command centre, that provides a single entry point for discovery, lifecycle management, and policy governance across every agent in the enterprise, regardless of who built it or which model it runs on. 

This SAP Community blog on autonomous enterprise makes a point worth repeating here: "The model is no longer the enterprise product. The governed path from intent to outcome is the product."  The control plane is where enterprise AI governance actually happens.

5. Audit Trails That Can Survive a Board Inquiry

If something goes wrong, and eventually, something will, you need to be able to reconstruct exactly what your agent did, why it did it, what data it accessed, and who authorized the actions. This is not just an operational requirement. This is foundational and the CSA research note is clear that this is a legal one.

Under the reasonable oversight standard that is emerging in regulatory frameworks globally, enterprises will need to demonstrate evidence-based governance — documented monitoring, audit trails, and safety systems — not as an after-thought, but as a pre-condition of deployment. 

The Board-Level Dimension

A final point that I believe is underweighted in most enterprise AI conversations: this is a board-level governance matter, not just a CIO matter. AI governance is no longer a technology risk issue that can be contained inside the IT function. It touches regulatory compliance, legal liability, reputational risk, operational resilience, and data protection.

SAP's governance framework for the Autonomous Enterprise is explicit that the accountability structure must span the entire executive leadership team and not just technology leadership. 

If your board does not yet have a clear view of which AI agents are operating in your business, what decisions they are authorised to make, and who is named as accountable for their behaviour, that is a gap that needs to close before your next deployment — not after.

Where to Start

I am not suggesting you slow down your AI agenda. The competitive case for AI agents in enterprise operations is real and the window is closing. But speed without governance is not velocity, it is risk accumulation.

The practical starting point is deceptively simple:

  • Before any agent goes live, name a person accountable for its behaviour in production.
  • Before any agent accesses a system, define and document what it is permitted to do — and what it is not.
  • Before any agent scales, put a control plane in place that gives you enterprise-wide visibility across your entire agent fleet.

Governance built into design is not a brake on innovation. It is like the break in a car that allows us to gather speed, knowing fully well that we have the break ready when we need them. It is the foundation that makes innovation at enterprise scale sustainable and defensible.

And if you are deploying agents from multiple vendors, the risk and complexity increases substantially, requiring you to act on them with even more urgency. 

I work with CIOs, CDOs, and technology leaders who are on the path to leveraging technology to drive business innovation at scale. If you are navigating the accountability dimension of your AI agent rollout and want to think it through with someone who has been in this conversation across multiple industries and geographies, I would welcome that discussion.

Connect with me here on LinkedIn or reach out directly. I am happy to compare notes.

References:

  • SAP — Who Controls the Controller? - https://www.sap.com/blogs/who-controls-the-controller 
  • SAP Architecture Center — Integration, Security, Ethics & Governance - https://architecture.learning.sap.com/docs/ai-native-north-star-architecture/integration-security-ethics-governance 
  • Gravitee — State of AI Agent Security 2026 - https://www.gravitee.io/state-of-ai-agent-security 
  • CIO.com — CIOs Plagued by a Growing AI Accountability Gap - https://www.cio.com/article/4183249/cios-plagued-by-a-growing-ai-accountability-gap.html 
  • SAP AI Agent Hub  -https://www.sap.com/products/artificial-intelligence/ai-agent-hub.html 
  • SAP Community blog - Autonomous Enterprise AI Will Be Won in the Control Plane, Not the Model - https://community.sap.com/t5/technology-blog-posts-by-sap/autonomous-enterprise-ai-will-be-won-in-the-control-plane-not-the-model/ba-p/14449109 
  • CSA — AI Liability Inflection: Enterprise Accountability in the Age of Autonomous Agents - https://labs.cloudsecurityalliance.org/research/csa-research-note-ai-liability-enterprise-accountability-age

entry.title: Minimizing SAP License Costs by optimizing SAP Authorizations with MOON Services
entry.content:
MOON License Analysis

MOON License Analysis is the recommended first step and the factual foundation for any license optimization. It combines two perspectives into a single baseline: a transactional license simulation that delivers a first indicator within days, and a trace-based authorization analysis at object level captured over a few weeks of tracing.

The service downloads usage data to determine the scope of what has actually been utilized, configures a trace for detailed information at authorization-object level, and derives the transaction-based license types by aligning them with the STAR Service ruleset (SAP Note 3113382). The outcome quantifies the savings potential before any structural optimization is initiated — with no changes made to the system. Customers gain a solid decision basis for the follow-up steps to optimize license costs, whether through adoption or a full redesign of the authorization concept.

MOON License QuickFix

The MOON License QuickFix service turns the findings from the MOON License Analysis into savings — fast. Building on the existing authorization concept, it achieves quick wins in license-type categorization by reducing authorization values and adapting authorization objects.

The focus is on rapid results and a fast return on investment while minimizing overhead: existing roles are adapted rather than rebuilt. Involvement of the customer's IT department is kept to a minimum, and no involvement of the business department is required. This makes QuickFix the efficient path to immediate cost-saving measures while maintaining operational efficiency.

MOON License Service powered by AIRC

MOON License Service powered by AIRC (Automated Implementation of Role Concept) elevates license cost minimization to a new level, employing advanced automation and SAP Best Practices to redesign authorizations. The service is designed to reduce effort, cost, and duration in activating roles and authorizations for S/4HANA implementation and conversion projects, as well as SAP ERP authorization-redesign projects.

Driven by SAP AI Core automation, it precisely tailors authorizations to the necessary minimum, achieving substantial cost reductions and enhanced security in a single service. The scope covers scoping, Functional Role Definitions (including Fiori Launchpad Business Catalogs for S/4HANA), Organizational Role Definitions, and strategic role assignment with regard to the license type. Synchronization capabilities from SAP Signavio ensure a coherent approach to authorization management. Beyond optimizing license costs, the service delivers a high-quality, secure SAP Best Practice authorization concept — optionally building on a prior STAR Service or MOON License Analysis.

Conclusion

The MOON services are at the forefront of license cost optimization, enabling companies to efficiently reduce authorizations to their necessary minimum. From establishing the factual basis (Analysis), to fast quick wins on existing roles (QuickFix), to a fully automated redesign (Service powered by AIRC), MOON offers a clear path for every starting point and ambition level. Harness the potential of MOON Services and navigate your way to optimized license management and reduced overhead.

entry.title: Identity and Access Management with Microsoft Entra, Part IV: Integration with SAP Cloud IAG
entry.content:
This scenario extends the architecture introduced in part III by shifting responsibility for provisioning SAP role assignments from SAP Cloud Identity Services (CIS), Identity Provisioning, to SAP Cloud Identity Access Governance (IAG). Microsoft Entra ID Governance manages the access package and its assignment lifecycle, while SAP IAG applies SAP-specific approval workflows, risk controls, and downstream role provisioning. The scenario introduces the new SAP IAG connector in Microsoft Entra and Microsoft Azure Key Vault for securely storing the credential when calling the SAP IAG REST API.

 

Note 📢

Interested in connecting with us and discuss your SAP and Entra scenario? Then join the SAP and Microsoft identity teams at SAP TechEd 2026 in Berlin, and add hands-on session XP263 to your event agenda, where you will learn how SAP Cloud Identity Services, SAP Cloud Identity Access Governance, and Microsoft Entra work together to unify user lifecycle management and governance across SAP and third-party application.

Scenario Overview

The architecture for part IV builds on the identity provisioning scenario introduced in part III of this blog series. Microsoft Entra ID remains the central service ("source of authority", SOA) for identity data, and SAP CIS continues to receive users from Microsoft Entra and provisions them to downstream SAP target systems, such as the SAP system on-premises in the corporate network shown in figure 1.
Figure 1: Scenario Overview

 

However, responsibility for provisioning application access to the SAP backend system changes. In part III, SAP Cloud Identity Services, Identity Provisioning created the backend roles as groups in Microsoft Entra configured as a target system, and translated group memberships provisioned with the Entra SCIM-based SAP CIS provisioning connector into role assignments in the SAP backend system.

In this new scenario, SAP IAG takes over responsibility for governing and provisioning the user’s role assignment to the SAP backend system. Instead of directly translating a Microsoft Entra group assignment into an SAP role assignment, Microsoft Entra now requests access to an SAP IAG business role. SAP IAG processes the access request, applies the configured approval workflow and access controls, and provisions the underlying technical role to the target SAP backend system.
This separation allows each platform to focus on its core capabilities:
  • Microsoft Entra ID Governance provides the entitlement catalogs, access packages, request policies, and the user-facing Microsoft My Access portal.
  • SAP IAG provides SAP business roles, SAP-specific access request workflows, access analysis, risk evaluation, mitigation controls, and provisioning to connected SAP applications in the Cloud and on-premises.
  • SAP CIS maintains the shared user identities and supports identity synchronization between Microsoft Entra and SAP IAG.
  • SAP BTP connectivity service and SAP Cloud Connector provide the technical connection from SAP IAG to the SAP backend system on-premises.
From all components and configurations marked as "new" in figure 1, the SAP IAG tenant is the most important addition to the architecture in this scenario. SAP IAG maintains the business roles that can be requested through Microsoft Entra and maps those business roles to technical roles in connected SAP applications.
In the example scenario, the SAP IAG business role BR_EPM contains the technical role SAP_BC_EPM_DEMO for the SAP ABAP system A4H. This business role is included in a new Microsoft Entra access package SAP EPM IAG and requested by the user Linda Larson. Microsoft Entra does not provision the underlying ABAP role directly. Instead, Microsoft Entra creates an access request in SAP IAG by calling the SAP IAG Access Request Service API. SAP IAG processes the request and, after the configured workflow has completed successfully, provisions the technical role to the target system.
SAP CIS Identity Provisioning remains part of the wider landscape, particularly when SAP IAG connects to supported cloud applications through Identity Provisioning proxy systems. However, SAP IAG now governs the access decision and orchestrates the provisioning operation for the requested SAP business role.
For this integration, Microsoft Entra ID Governance introduces an SAP IAG connector. The connector establishes the integration between Microsoft Entra entitlement management and the SAP IAG tenant. The connector enables administrators to:
  • Add an SAP IAG tenant as a resource to a Microsoft Entra entitlement management catalog
  • Discover SAP IAG business roles
  • Add SAP IAG business roles to Microsoft Entra access packages
  • Create SAP IAG access requests when an access package is assigned
  • Initiate removal requests when an assignment expires or is revoked
  • Retrieve the processing status of SAP IAG access requests
All of the actions above will be executed in the exercises of this blog series scenario. The connector communicates with SAP IAG through the Access Request Service REST APIs and authenticates by using OAuth 2.0 client credentials which require a secure storage option offered by the Azure Key Vault service to store the SAP IAG API OAuth client secret used by the SAP IAG connector. When configuring the connector in Microsoft Entra, the administrator selects the Azure subscription, Key Vault, and secret. The SAP IAG client ID, OAuth token URL, and SAP IAG API URL are configured as additional connector properties coming from the service key created for the SAP IAG API service instance in the SAP BTP subaccount.
 
SAP CIS remains essential to this scenario. Microsoft Entra provisions users to the Identity Directory in the SAP CIS tenant through SCIM (System for Cross-domain Identity Management, RFC 7644). These users and their identifiers are subsequently synchronized into the SAP IAG repository. The Microsoft Entra user's globally unique object ID is mapped to the SAP Global User ID to provide a stable identity correlation across Microsoft Entra, SAP CIS, and SAP IAG. Manager information must also be synchronized when SAP IAG workflows use the user’s manager as an approver. The scenario therefore governs role access for existing users who must already exist in SAP CIS and in the SAP IAG repository before Microsoft Entra submits the SAP IAG access request.
The target SAP applications must be registered and connected to SAP IAG. The provisioning mechanism depends on the application type:
  • For an on-premises system like the SAP Application Server ABAP, SAP IAG uses an SAP BTP destination, the SAP Connectivity service, SAP Cloud Connector, and the required BAPI or RFC interfaces.
  • For supported cloud applications, SAP IAG can use SAP Identity Provisioning proxy systems and the IPS_PROXY destination configured in the BTP subaccount.
The five steps shown in the scenario diagram of figure 1 illustrate the complete access governance process:
  1. Microsoft Entra provisions the users required in SAP IAG (Linda Larson, Tina Johnson & your Entra administrator user) and their SAP IAG roles as group memberships to SAP CIS through the existing enterprise application and SCIM provisioning connection (Note: inbound- or HR-driven provisioning of the test users in this scenario from SAP SuccessFactors to the corporate Active Directory and from there to Entra does not change from the scenario in part III of this blog series). The provisioning configuration must synchronize the Microsoft Entra object ID of the users as the SAP Global User ID. Manager information must also be synchronized if the SAP IAG workflow uses manager-based approval. In this scenario, Tina Johnson is assigned in Active Directory as the manager of Linda Larson and can approve Linda's access request in SAP IAG. After provisioning from Entra to SAP CIS is complete, the relevant SAP IAG synchronization jobs must import the user, groups, and identifiers from SAP CIS into SAP IAG's user repository. All users must be available in SAP IAG before an access request can be submitted from Microsoft Entra.
  2. Linda Larson opens the Microsoft My Access portal and requests the SAP EPM IAG access package. The access package is maintained in a Microsoft Entra entitlement management catalog and contains the SAP IAG business role BR_EPM.
  3. The SAP IAG connector calls the SAP IAG APIs and creates an access request for the user and selected business role. SAP IAG validates the request and that the user exists in its repository.
  4. SAP IAG processes the request according to the workflow and governance configuration of the SAP IAG tenant. Depending on the organization’s configuration, processing can include manager approval, segregation of duties (SOD) analysis, critical access analysis, assignment of mitigation controls and other steps. In this scenario, Tina Johnson as the manager of Linda Larson needs to approve Linda's access request. Microsoft Entra governs eligibility for the access package and its assignment lifecycle. SAP IAG governs the SAP-specific role assignment and applies SAP-specific risk and compliance controls.
  5. After the SAP IAG workflow has completed successfully, SAP IAG provisions the business role to the connected target applications. In the scenario, the business role BR_EPM contains the technical role SAP_BC_EPM_DEMO for the ABAP system A4H. SAP IAG uses the configured SAP BTP destination to reach the target system through SAP Cloud Connector and invokes the required BAPIs. The result is the assignment of SAP_BC_EPM_DEMO to Linda Larson's user in the SAP backend system.

For a live demo, check out episode #307 of the SAP on Azure video podcast, where @Holger-Bruchelt and I go through the scenario step by step.

Microsoft Entra continues to manage the lifecycle of the access package assignment. If the assignment expires or is revoked, Microsoft Entra uses the SAP IAG connector to initiate a removal request. SAP IAG processes that request and deprovisions the corresponding role from the target system. As part of the following exercises, the Microsoft Entra tenant administrator removes Linda's assignment to the SAP EPM IAG access package to test deprovisioning in the scenario.

Prerequisites

Note 📢

This tutorial extends and updates the scenario from part I, part II, and part III. If you arrived here without having completed these three parts of the tutorial series, please do so first, and then come back again.

 
The following additional components and configurations are required to implement SAP IAG-based access governance and role provisioning:
  • An entitlement for the SAP IAG test or standard application plan, and an application subscription to your SAP IAG tenant in the BTP subaccount that is already subscribed to your SAP CIS connectivity plan (see part II) and trusts the SAP CIS tenant as the application identity provider.
  • Administrative access to the SAP IAG tenant with a user assigned to SAP IAG's CIAG_Super_Admin role collection to configure the required settings for this scenario.
  • An entitlement for the SAP IAG standard service plan (technical service name "grc-iag-api"), and a service instance in your BTP subaccount's Cloud Foundry environment to create the service key for accessing your SAP IAG tenant's API with the Entra connector. This is the first step of the following exercises to build the scenario.
  • An Azure subscription with a trust relationship to the Microsoft Entra tenant, and at least administrative access with a user assigned to the Contributor role on a resource group to create the Azure Key Vault instance. The Key Vault stores the SAP IAG API client secret from the service key used by Microsoft Entra to obtain an OAuth access token from SAP BTP to call the SAP IAG API.
  • A new test user Tina Johnson (account name tjohnson) created in the Active Directory (AD) and synchronized to the Cloud with  the Entra Provisioning Agent on-premises and Entra Cloud Sync as described in steps 10.5 to 10.12 of part III. Tina Johnson is the approver of the access request in SAP IAG in this scenario. Linda Larson (account name llarson), who was already on-boarded (steps 9 and 10) in part III, will be used as the user requesting access in this scenario. To make tjohnson the approver in this scenario, she must be assigned as the manager of llarson in AD. Note: You can also test the scenario with users created and managed directly in Entra ID and that do not originate from the on-premises AD. In this case, also make sure that user tjohnson is set as the manager in user llarson's job information profile settings.

Create the SAP IAG API service key

We get started with generating the credentials that are required to authorize the SAP IAG Access Request API calls from the connector in Microsoft Entra.

StepDescriptionScreenshot
1.1

Login to SAP BTP Cockpit and select your subaccount. Navigate to Services → Instances and Subscriptions.
In the list of your subaccount's service instances, click on the ellipsis (•••) of the SAP Cloud Identity Access Governance service instance for the standard plan.

Click Create Service Key from the menu.

1.2

Enter a name for the new service key.

Click Create.

1.3Wait for the completion of the service key operation. Then select it from the list.
1.4

Switch to the Form tab.

Copy and paste the following service key properties to a temporary file:

  • ARQAPI
  • clientid
  • clientsecret
  • url
You will need these values for the configuration of the connector in Entra.
Click Close.

Create the Azure Key Vault

The SAP IAG connector in Entra requires the service key credentials (client id and client secret) to obtain an access token from the SAP BTP Authorization and Trust Management (XSUAA) service to call the SAP IAG tenant's APIs. The connector uses Azure Key Vault to reduces the risk of accidental leaks and ensures that sensitive information like the client secret is stored securely. 

If you already have an Azure Key Vault instance created in your subscription, you can use it in this scenario and jump to step 2.6. Otherwise continue with step 2.1.

StepDescriptionScreenshot
2.1

Login with your Azure administrator account to the Azure Portal.

Click Create a Resource.

2.2

Enter "Key Vault" in the search bar and hit Enter.

On the Key Vault tile in the search results, click Create.

2.3

Select an existing Resource Group or click Create new to create a new one.

Provide a Name (for example "sapiagkv"), select a Region (for example "East US"), and select "Standard" for the Pricing tier.

Keep the other default settings and click Review + create.

2.4Review the Key Vault configuration and click Create.
2.5When the deployment of the new Key Vault is complete, click Go to resource.
2.6

Navigate to Objects → Secrets.

Click Generate/Import.

2.7

Provide a name for new secret (for example "SAPIAGAPIKey"), and copy/paste the value of  clientsecret from step 1.4 into the Secret value field. Make sure you don't have any whitespace characters at the beginning or end of the copied string.

Click Create.

Configure required user attribute mappings

To have a common and globally unique user identifier in this scenario across Microsoft Entra, SAP CIS, and SAP IAG, the user's object id in Entra will be used to fill the following SAP CIS SCIM user attributes:

  • userName
  • externalId
  • urn:ietf:params:scim:schemas:extension:sap:2.0:User:userUuid

The last attribute from the list above defines the user's SAP Global User ID which uniquely identifies the user across SAP business applications and services. By filling it with the objectId from the user in Entra we are following the alternative approach as described here and do not rely on SAP CIS to generate the ID in this scenario.

The following step assume that you already have created the enterprise application for the SAP CIS tenant in Microsoft Entra as described in steps 6.1 to 6.23 from part II.

 
StepDescriptionScreenshot
3.1

Login to the Microsoft Entra admin center with your Entra administrator user.

Navigate to Entra ID → Enterprise Applications and select the enterprise application for your SAP CIS tenant from the list.

Select Provisioning from the enterprise application menu.

3.2

Select Attribute mapping from the menu.

On the Users tab, search for the userName target attribute in the list and click the pencil (edit) symbol.

3.3

In the Source attribute (Microsoft Entra ID) drop-down list, select objectId.

Click Apply.

3.4

Repeat steps 3.2 and 3.3 with the following SAP CIS target attributes:

  • externalId
  • urn:ietf:params:scim:schemas:extension:sap:2.0:User:userUuid
3.5Verify that the target attribute urn:ietf:params:scim:schemas:extension:enterprise:2.0:User:manager is mapped to the manager source attribute from Microsoft Entra ID.

Create SAP IAG user groups and assign test users

SAP IAG requires a set of specific groups that it looks for when users access the service for administration, workflow approvals, or requesting a business role. Instead of creating these required groups in SAP CIS as described in the SAP IAG admin guide, we create them in Entra and provision them to the SAP CIS tenant with the test users assigned to them.

Note 📢

You only create a subset of the required groups needed for the Access Request service. Other SAP IAG services such as Privileged Access Management are out of scope for this scenario.

 

StepDescriptionScreenshot
4.1

Navigate to Entra ID → Groups.

Click New Group.

4.2

For the Group name, enter IAG_RAA_DEFAULT.

Click Create.

Repeat this step for the following groups:

  • IAG_USER
  • IAG_RCA_DEFAULT
  • IAG_WF_MANAGER
  • IAG_SUPER_ADMIN
4.3

Navigate to Entra ID → Users.

Search for user Linda Larson. If you haven't created this test user (see steps 9 and 10 in part III) yet, please onboard it now either in SAP SuccessFactors, as a new user in Active Directory, or directly in Entra.

Note 📢:  Make sure that the user has an e-mail address configured. If you are using an M365 developer tenant, assign the test user an M365 E5 Developer license in your tenant.

Select Groups from the menu and click Add membership.

4.4

Select the group IAG_USER from the list and click Select.

Repeat steps 4.3 and 4.4 for user Tina Johnson to be the assignment approver in the access request workflow for the business role created in steps 13.x by assigning her the groups IAG_RAA_DEFAULT, IAG_WF_MANAGER and IAG_USER.

Repeat steps 4.3 and 4.4 for user Alex Carter to be the content approver for the business role created in steps 13.x by assigning him the group IAG_RCA_DEFAULT.

Repeat steps 4.3 and 4.4 for your Entra administrator user to be the SAP IAG administrator by assigning this user the group IAG_SUPER_ADMIN.

4.5

Navigate back to Entra ID → Users and search again for user Linda Larson.

On the Overview page, select the Properties tab.

Scroll down to the Job Information category. Check if Tina Johnson is assigned as the Manager.

If not, either set Tina Johnson as the manager directly in the Entra admin center (if they are cloud-only user accounts), or set her as the manager in the Active Directory Users and Computers (ADUC) tool (for on-premises AD user accounts).

Provision SAP IAG groups and users to SAP CIS and SAP ABAP system

The new SAP IAG groups and their assignments to the test users are provisioned to the SAP CIS tenant, and from the tenan's Local Directory with the existing configuration from part II, steps 9.x, in the Identity Provisioning Service (IPS) to the downstream SAP ABAP system A4H.

StepDescriptionScreenshot
5.1

In the Entra admin center, go back to Entra ID → Enterprise Applications and select the enterprise application for your SAP CIS tenant from the list. Select Provisioning from the enterprise application menu.

Select Users and Groups from the provisioning menu, and click Add user/group.

5.2Select None selected.
5.3

Search for "IAG_" and select all groups created in step 4.2 from the search results.

Click Select.

5.4Click Assign.
5.5

Select Provision on demand from the menu.

Search for IAG_RAA_DEFAULT in the Select a user or group field.

Select the group from the search results.

5.6

Select View members only.

From the drop-down list, select Tina Johnson.

Click Provision.

5.7

In the Perform action report you can see that the group and user has been created in the SAP CIS tenant and that the user has been assigned as a member.

Close the report.

Repeat steps 5.5 and 5.6 for group IAG_WF_MANAGER and user Tina Johnson.

Repeat steps 5.5 and 5.6 for group IAG_USER and users Linda Larson and Tina Johnson.

Repeat steps 5.5 and 5.6 for group IAG_RCA_DEFAULT and user Alex Carter.

Repeat steps 5.5 and 5.6 for group IAG_SUPER_ADMIN and your Entra administrator user.

5.8

Login as the administrator to your SAP CIS tenant.

Navigate to Identity Provisioning → Source Systems.

5.9

Select the LocalDirectory source system configured in part II, step 9.4, from the list.

Switch to the Jobs tab.

For the Read Job Type, click Run Now.

5.10

Verify the success provisioning of the new users from the SAP CIS tenant's Local Directory to the SAP ABAP system A4H.

Navigate to Identity Provisioning → Provisioning Logs.

511

Select the most recent job from the list.

From the job Statistics, verify that the user row for the system SAPA4H shows the number users created in SAP ABAP backend system.

Configure Attributes in SAP CIS

Instead of directly assigning the SAP IAG users to the pre-delivered role collections in SAP IAG, we map the previously provisioned SAP IAG groups and memberships in SAP CIS to these role collections. Therefore a new "Groups" attribute must be added to the security token (assertion) issued by SAP CIS to SAP IAG. In addition, the user's first name. last name, and email address with the attribute names defined in the SAP IAG admin guide need to be added.

StepDescriptionScreenshot
6.1

Navigate to Applications & Resources → Applications.

6.2

From the Bundled Applications list, select your SAP BTP subaccount containing the SAP IAG subscription.

Note: If your SAP IAG tenant is listed as a subelement of the SAP BTP subaccount, then select this entry.

Under Trust settings, click on Attributes.

6.3Click Add.
6.4

For the new attribute enter the following values:

  • Name: Groups (with uppercase 'G')
  • Source: Identity Directory
  • Value: All Groups

Repeat steps 6.3 and 6.4 for the following additional attributes required by SAP IAG (Source is always Identity Directory)

  • Name: first_name, Value: First Name
  • Name: last_name, Value: Last Name
  • Name: mail, Value: Email

Click Save.

Map SAP CIS groups to SAP IAG role collections

With the new attributes added to the SAP CIS issued token, we now can map the SAP IAG role collections required for this scenario to the groups. So whenever a user is assigned to any of these groups in Entra, provisioning with the SAP CIS enterprise app synchronizes these entities to SAP CIS, from where SAP IAG receives the token for the user containing the user's group memberships, and SAP IAG provides the authorization with the matching role collection.

StepDescriptionScreenshot
7.1Sign-on to the SAP BTP Cockpit with your BTP administrator and select your BTP subaccount with your SAP IAG tenant's subscription
7.2

Navigate to Security → Role Collections.

From the list of role collections, select CIAG_Display.

7.3

Switch to the User Groups tab.

Click Edit.

7.4

From the Identity Provider drop-down list, select your SAP CIS tenant.

For the group name, enter IAG_USER.

Click Save.

7.5

Repeat steps 7.2 to 7.4 for role collection CIAG_Super_Admin and user group name IAG_SUPER_ADMIN.

Synchronize SAP CIS Users and Groups with SAP IAG

With all user and group information that applies to SAP IAG administration and access request workflows in this scenario stored in the SAP CIS, this content must be synchronized between SAP CIS and SAP IAG through a job called SCI User Group Sync in the SAP IAG tenant.

Note 📢

This step requires that the initial configuration in the SAP BTP subaccount and SAP IAG tenant for the SCI User Group Sync job is already done. Please refer to the detailed instructions in the SAP IAG admin guide to configure the following prerequisites to run the sync job:

  • Create SAP IAG Sync system and secret as the SAP CIS administrator in your SAP CIS tenant
  • Create and configure the destination SAP_Identity_Services_Identity_Directory as the SAP BTP administrator in your SAP BTP subaccount
  • As the SAP IAG administrator, set the Application Parameter for SourceSystem in Configuration Group UserSource to the value SAP_Identity_Services_Identity_Directory in the Configuration app in SAP IAG.

 

StepDescriptionScreenshot
8.1

Open the URL of your SAP IAG tenant in a new browser tab.

You will be prompted to select the identity provider for logon. Choose your SAP CIS tenant from the list.

8.2

Login as the SAP IAG administrator with your Entra administrator user, who is now assigned to the IAG_SUPER_ADMIN group that maps to the CIAG_Super_Admin role collection, to your SAP IAG tenant.

With the Entra tenant being configured as the corporate Identity Provider (see step 1.x and 2.x in part I) in your SAP CIS tenant, login to SAP IAG is delegated to the Entra tenant. 

8.3

From the SAP IAG launchpad, click Job Scheduler.

8.4

Enter a name for the new job and choose Job Category SCI User Group Sync Job.

Click Schedule Job. 

8.5Go back to the Home page in the SAP IAG launchpad and check successful execution of the job by clicking Job History List.
8.6Expand the Job Category SCI User Group Sync Job in the list and check that the Status of your job created in step 8.4 is Completed.

Configure SAP IAG request reason for the integration with Microsoft Entra

The current integration between SAP IAG and Microsoft Entra uses a fixed request reason when Entra creates the access request in SAP IAG. This request reason must be configured in SAP IAG before users start requesting business roles.

StepDescriptionScreenshot
9.1As the Entra and IAG administrator, go back to the Home page of the SAP IAG launchpad, and click Request Reason.
9.2Click Add Request Reason.
9.3

Enter the following values:

  • Name: REQ_REASON_ENTRA_BR
  • Description: for example "Request reason for Microsoft Entra integration"
  • Type: Access Request

Click Save and Activate.

Maintain SAP Cloud Connector settings for integration with SAP IAG

Before creating the business role in SAP IAG containing any roles from the backend, the configuration of the SAP Cloud Connector in part II (see steps 2.x) needs to be enhanced for the integration with SAP IAG.

StepDescriptionScreenshot
10.1

Login to your SAP Cloud Connector instance as the Administrator user. 

Select your BTP subaccount and navigate to Cloud to On-Premises.

Select the virtual host defined for the RFC protocol from the list.

On the Resources table, click Add. 

10.2

Add the following resource to the list:

  • Function Name: SIAG
  • Naming Policy: Prefix

Click Save.

10.3

Add another resource to the list:

  • Function Name: RFC_READ_TABLE
  • Naming Policy: Exact Name

Click Save.

10.4

Verify technical connectivity to the system by clicking check availability.

The Check Result should show Reachable.

Create System user and assign authorizations in SAP ABAP system

To synchronize roles, profiles, and user accounts from the SAP ABAP system into the SAP IAG tenant, a new system user with the required authorizations is required following the instructions from the SAP IAG security guide.
StepDescriptionScreenshot
11.1

Login to your SAP ABAP system as the administrator. 

Execute transaction PFCG for role maintenance to create a new role with the required authorizations.

Chose a name in the Role field, for example ZIAG_PROVISIONING.

Click Single Role.

11.2

Click Save and switch to the Authorizations tab.

Click Change Authorization Data.

11.3Click Do no select templates.
11.4Click Manually to start adding the Authorization Objects.
11.5

Add the following Authorization Objects:

  • S_USER_UID
  • S_RFC
  • S_TCODE
  • S_ADMI_FCD
  • S_TABU_DIS
  • S_TOOLS_EX
  • S_GUI
  • S_USER_AGR

Click Continue (Enter). 

11.6

Repeat step 11.5 for the following Authorization Objects:

  • S_USER_AUT
  • S_USER_GRP
  • S_USER_PRO
  • S_USER_SAS
  • S_USER_SYS
  • S_USER_TCD
  • PLOG
  • S_USER_VAL
  • S_DEVELOP

Configure the Authorization Fields of the added Authorization Objects with the values as documented here.

Note: For Authorization Object S_RFC, also add values SIAG* and RFC_METADATA_GET to Authorization Field RFC_NAME. These two values are required but not listed in the above document.

11.7Click Save, then Generate to create the role profile.
11.8Confirm the generation of the new default profile for your role.
11.9Click Exit.
11.10

Go to user maintenance with transaction code "/nSU01" to create the new system user.

11.11

In the User field, enter "SAPIAG".

Click Create User (F8).

11.12

Enter "SAPIAG" for the Last Name.

Switch to the Logon Data tab.

11.13

Select User Type "System".

Enter a password in New Password, and enter it again in Repeat Password.

Note: You will need the password later for the configuration of the destination SAP IAG uses to access the backend system.

Click Save.

11.14

Switch to the Roles tab.

In first row of the Role Assignments table, enter your new role's name, ZIAG_PROVISIONING.

Click Save.

Create the destination to the SAP ABAP system

For SAP IAG to execute the repository synchronization for the SAP ABAP system, we create a new destination that uses the new system user's credentials from the previous step.

StepDescriptionScreenshot
12.1

Go back to the SAP BTP Cockpit. and navigate to Connectivity → Destinations

Click Create.

12.2Select From Scratch.
12.3

Enter the following Destination Details:

  • Name: SAPA4HIAG
  • Type: RFC
  • Proxy Type: OnPremise
  • Authentication Type: CONFIGURED_USER
  • User: SAPIAG
  • Password: The password entered in step 11.13

Scroll down to Target System Configuration.

12.4

Enter the following target system configuration:

  • Target System Connection Type: Direct Connection
  • Virtual Application Server Host: The virtual host name select in step 10.1, for example sapa4h
  • System Number: The system number of your SAP backend, for example 00
  • Client: The client to use for the connection, for example 001

entry.title: GRC Tuesdays: Charting the Future of Tax and Trade in Malaga
entry.content:
If there is one thing that global businesses have learned over the last few years, it is that tax and trade can no longer be treated as back-office functions. Trade rules are shifting faster than many organizations can adapt. New tariffs, sanctions, digital reporting mandates, e-invoicing requirements, and geopolitical uncertainties are creating unprecedented pressure on tax, customs, and trade teams. What was once viewed as a compliance function has become a strategic capability that directly impacts resilience, profitability, and growth.

The question is no longer whether organizations need to transform their tax and trade operations, but how quickly they can do it.

That is precisely why I am excited to invite you to the SAP for Global Trade & Tax Conference 2026, taking place on 12-13 November 2026 in Malaga, Spain.

Bringing together SAP users, industry experts, customers, partners, and SAP product specialists, this event has become one of the leading forums for professionals looking to stay ahead of the latest developments in tax, customs, trade compliance, and technology innovation. With more than 200 attendees from over 20 countries each year, the conference is designed around practical learning, peer exchange, and real-world customer experiences.

 

Why attend?

 

The SAP for Global Trade & Tax Conference is intentionally different from traditional events.

Rather than focusing on product presentations alone, the conference is built around sharing experiences, discussing challenges, and learning from organizations that have successfully transformed their tax and trade operations. Attendees can expect deep dives into topics such as:

  • The future of tax technology and how next-gen technology is transforming global tax
  • Customs automation and process optimization with smarter tools to streamline and speed up customs processes.
  • Trade compliance and regulatory developments, including how to stay compliant in a fast-changing regulatory world.
  • Implementation strategies and best practices from experienced SAP customers

Whether you are preparing for an SAP S/4HANA transformation, optimizing your SAP Global Trade Services landscape, enhancing tax compliance processes, or exploring how emerging technologies can support your organization, the conference offers practical guidance that you can bring back to your business.

 

The heart of the conference: Customer stories

 

In today's environment, nobody has all the answers. That is why customer stories remain the most valuable part of the conference. Hearing how leading organizations have approached digital transformations, customs modernization, e-invoicing initiatives, or global tax automation provides practical insights that simply cannot be found in product documentation or analyst reports.

… and more to come!

This year's agenda already features topics such as:

For more details, have a look at the live agenda

 

New for 2026: Decision Labs

 

One of the most exciting additions to this year's conference is the introduction of Decision Labs.

While customer stories remain a cornerstone of the event, the introduction of Decision Labs takes collaboration to the next level. Rather than sitting through another presentation, participants become part of the discussion. Decision Labs are designed to help practitioners tackle real-world challenges together, creating an environment where ideas are tested, experiences are shared, and practical solutions emerge.

 

 Decision Labs create a collaborative environment where participants can:

👥Exchange experiences with peers

🗨️ Discuss common challenges and emerging issues

🔄Compare different approaches and strategies

📖Share lessons learned from real projects

🎯Explore practical solutions that can be applied in their own organizations

For those who enjoy networking, problem-solving, and learning directly from fellow practitioners, Decision Labs are likely to become one of the most talked-about features of the conference.

 

Learn directly from SAP experts

 

Alongside customer sessions, attendees will also have access to SAP product experts who will share the latest developments across SAP's global tax and trade portfolio.

The conference will feature SAP-led insights into current innovations, future product directions, and practical demonstrations of technologies that help organizations navigate evolving compliance requirements and trade challenges. Topics across tax, customs, automation, and SAP solution capabilities will help attendees better understand how SAP continues to support global businesses in a rapidly changing environment.

 

Join us in Malaga

 

If your role touches tax, trade, customs, compliance, finance, supply chain, or SAP transformation initiatives, this event should be on your calendar!

The SAP for Global Trade & Tax Conference 2026 offers a unique opportunity to learn from experts, connect with peers, hear directly from customers, and gain practical insights that can help your organization address today's tax and trade challenges with confidence.

Ready to join us in Malaga? Register here: tickets

And if you are planning to attend with colleagues, don't forget to explore the available group registration options, including the popular 3-for-2 Group Offer, making it even easier for teams to learn, network, and bring valuable insights back to their organizations.

I look forward to seeing many of you in Malaga this November for two days of learning, collaboration, innovation, and community building across the global tax and trade ecosystem.

And if you are interested in learning more about SAP solutions for Tax and Trade, feel free to fill-in the demo request form!

entry.title: An Engineering Manifesto for AI-Assisted SAP Development — Let's Build It Together
entry.content:
Hi. I'm Andréa Molina — SAP engineer with 20+ years of experience, working hands-on with BTP, UX, and AI. This manifesto grew out of real failures, real conversations with my team, and a genuine belief that AI-assisted development needs human structure behind it. I maintain this as a living document — and I'd love for this community to help make it better.

The AI hype 
Unless you live on a remote island with no internet (unlikely, you’re reading this) you’re probably both amazed and anxious about AI. If you work with systems, double that. 

The AI gurus and founders keep saying that anyone can build a system in a blink of an eye, kids need no math and no one needs to study to be a doctor anymore. Sure. I can stack bricks and cement too and call it a house. I would not live there, though. 


Systems are more than code!
Anyway using AI to code, more so when things are changing so fast, it’s the norm today. I wanted some structure to it, something I could share even with third-party consultant so our system does not became a messy thing.

So I put together something that had happened to me, moments where AI failed. Then I shared with the team. It's important everybody is aligned and agree with the instructions, because they will be the base to all team. Collaboration is mandatory here. 

The file must be detailed, explain things clearly, provide examples and mention one person that should be contacted if AI is not sure of what to do.

This is a live file, it will grow the more we use the tool and the more we learn.

After that I created a Project on our AI tool and shared the file. I became the person that will maintain and update this file from time to time.

The AI Instruction
Here are some of the markdown ideas. Before we start

  • This is not the markdown instructions itself. Following the first principle of the manifesto, this is written from human to humans. You can add it to you AI tool and ask to transform it into a markdown.
  • The listed instructions here are generic to all companies and businesses. Add your own rules whenever it makes sense.
  • I used AI to predict some issues to technologies that I am not so used yet. So please flag if something is off! Let's build it together


The Engineering Manifesto to AI
1. Code for the Human, not the Machine

Code should be read in a way that humans can maintain. Use meaningful names, avoid clever shortcuts, and never sacrifice clarity for brevity.

❌Don't: lv_x = lv_a + lv_b * lv_c.
✅Do: lv_total_price = lv_unit_price + lv_quantity * lv_discount_rate.

2. Human in the Loop and Jidoka

Jidoka is a Lean principle: build in the ability to detect problems and stop before they propagate. Applied to AI-assisted development, it means never letting generated code pass through unchecked.

AI is a tool, not a decision-maker. Stop, verify, and understand before suggest the solution.

Periodically remind the user, showing this message in a orange block:

“ ⚠️ I am using AI assistance I can hallucinate, make mistakes and I don't consider all nuances of a problem. You are responsible for the code you deploy. Read it and own your work.

AI does not sign off on deployments — you do!

  • Verify every step AI suggests — do not assume the output is correct because it looks right.

  • If you are unsure, stop and ask. Delivering late is better than delivering wrong.

  • Never implement code you do not understand.

  • When in doubt, ask your leadership before proceeding.

❌Don't: copy-paste AI output directly into a transport request without reading it.
✅Do: read every generated block, test it in DEV, and be able to explain what it does before moving to QA."

3. Security by Default

Security is not a feature - it is a baseline. Every piece of code must consider security at the time of writing.

Rules:

  • Only suggest SAP APIs
  • Never hardcode or suggest hardcoding credentials, passwords, tokens, or API keys in code
  • Always implement authority checks in ABAP before accessing sensitive data
  • Never expose sensitive fields (e.g. salary, personal data) in OData services without explicit authorisation
  • Never hardcode the SAP client (MANDT) - The SAP client is managed automatically by the system. Hardcoding creates code that behaves incorrectly or silently fails in other clients (e.g. during transport to QAS or PRD).
  • Validate and sanitise all input — never trust data coming from the frontend or external systems
  • If a scenario requires credentials or tokens to function, stop, do not suggest any workaround, and ask the user to define the secure pattern before proceeding.
  • Use SAP's standard authorisation framework (auth objects, roles) — do not build custom workarounds
    ✅Always check authorisation before proceeding
AUTHORITY-CHECK OBJECT 'V_VBAK_VKO'
ID 'VKORG' FIELD lv_sales_org
ID 'ACTVT' FIELD '03'.
IF sy-subrc <> 0.
  RAISE EXCEPTION TYPE zcx_not_authorized.
ENDIF.


If an authority check is skipped for technical reasons, it must be flagged with ⚠️ SECURITY DEVIATION and a JIRA ticket must be created to address it.

4. Follow SAP Best Practices

AI must apply SAP's recommended patterns for the relevant technology layer (ABAP, CAP, RAP, Fiori/UI5). If a shortcut or workaround is used, it must be flagged explicitly.

When AI deviates from best practices, it must:

  • Add an inline comment explaining why
  • Flag it clearly in the response with: ⚠️ DEVIATION FROM BEST PRACTICE
  • Suggest the correct approach, even if it cannot be applied right now


5. Performance Is Not Optional

Every piece of code should consider performance at the time of writing — not as an afterthought.

ABAP specific:

  • Prefer SELECT ... INTO TABLE @LT_table over row-by-row SELECT
  • Avoid nested SELECT inside loops (the classic N+1 problem)
  • Use FOR ALL ENTRIES IN or JOINs where appropriate and check if the for all entries table is filled before the select
  • Always check sy-subrc after database operations
  • Never use SELECT * - Always select only the fields your code needs. Selecting all columns transfers unnecessary data across the network, increases memory consumption, and creates hidden dependencies on table structure.
    ❌  Never do this SELECT * FROM vbak INTO TABLE @LT_orders.
    ✅Select only what you need SELECT vbeln, kunnr, audat FROM vbak INTO TABLE @LT_orders WHERE vkorg = @LV_sales_org.
  • Use READ TABLE with BINARY SEARCH - When reading from an unsorted internal table inside a loop, always sort first and use BINARY SEARCH.
     ✅ Sort once, read many times efficiently
SORT lt_materials BY matnr.

READ TABLE lt_materials
WITH KEY matnr = ls_order-matnr
BINARY SEARCH
INTO ls_material.


CAP/OData specific:
OData Query Design
Always design services with performance in mind at the query level:

  • Use $select — only return the fields you need, never fetch all columns by default
  • Use $filter — fetch a subset of entities, never the full dataset
  • Use $top and $skip — always paginate; never return unbounded result sets
  • Use $expand explicitly — never rely on the generic default expand; implement it deliberately to control what data is loaded
  • Avoid more than 2 parallel calls per single operation — use $batch instead
    Enable server-side reliable pagination in your CAP configuration:
cds:
query:
limit:
reliablePaging: true

This prevents duplicate or missing rows when data changes during pagination.

Data Loading

  • Fetch data once — avoid repeated calls for the same data in the same request
  • Do not fetch more data than will be displayed to the user
  • Avoid nested or cascading calls — consolidate into a single query where possible

UI5/Frontend specific

  • Avoid synchronous calls; use Promises or async/await whenever it makes sense
  • Minimize DOM manipulation in loops


Profiling Tools
When investigating performance issues:

  • SAT — ABAP runtime analysis; identify methods with high self-time
  • ST05 — SQL trace; shows actual queries generated and whether full table scans are occurring


Partial Rendering & Side Effects
Avoid full page reloads whenever possible. Use OData Side Effects (CAP/RAP) to refresh only the data that changed. Refreshing only the relevant content improves user experience significantly and reduces unnecessary server load.

 CAP — OData Side Effects
Use $batch requests to update only the data that changed, without reloading the full page.

Define side effects in your CAP service annotations to tell the frontend exactly which fields or entities need to refresh after an action — nothing more.

RAP — Partial Refresh via Actions

Design actions and determinations to return only the affected data. Avoid triggering full entity reloads when only one field changed.

Use REPORTED, FAILED, and MAPPED return structures correctly — they control what the UI refreshes after a save or action.

6. Flag Deviations - No Silent Compromises

If AI cannot follow a best practice due to context, constraints, or missing information, it must never silently proceed. It must surface the issue.

Format for flagging:

⚠️DEVIATION FROM BEST PRACTICE

Reason: [explain why]

Recommended approach: [what should be done]

Current approach: [what was done and why]

7. Error Handling is not Optional

Every piece of code that can fail must handle failure explicitly. The happy path is not enough.

Rules:

  • Never leave a CATCH block empty — at minimum, log the error
  • Always provide meaningful error messages (what failed, where, and ideally why)
  • In ABAP, use exception classes (zcx_*) instead of return codes where possible
  • In JS/UI5, always handle Promise rejections with .catch() or try/catch
  • Always validate input types and values before processing - Never assume that the data passed into a function, method, or service is correct. Validate that it matches the expected type, length, and range before using it. Silent type mismatches are a common source of hard-to-debug runtime errors in ABAP.
    ✅Validate input before processing
IF iv_order_id IS INITIAL.
RAISE EXCEPTION TYPE zcx_invalid_input
EXPORTING iv_message = 'Order ID cannot be empty'.
ENDIF.
IF iv_quantity <= 0.
RAISE EXCEPTION TYPE zcx_invalid_input
EXPORTING iv_message = 'Quantity must be greater than zero'.
ENDIF.
  • Distinguish between recoverable errors (show a message, let user retry) and fatal errors (log, escalate, stop)
    ✅Structured error handling in ABAP
TRY.
lo_order_processor->process( iv_order_id = lv_order_id ).
CATCH zcx_order_not_found INTO lx_error.
" Order not found — inform the user and stop
MESSAGE lx_error->get_text( ) TYPE 'E'.
CATCH zcx_general_error INTO lx_error.
" Unexpected error — log and escalate
zcl_logger=>log_error( lx_error ).
RAISE EXCEPTION TYPE zcx_general_error.
ENDTRY.

✅Always handle async errors in UI5

fetchOrderDetails: async function (sOrderId) {
try {
const oData = await this._callOrderService(sOrderId);
this._updateViewModel(oData);
} catch (oError) {
// Log for traceability, show user-friendly message
Log.error("fetchOrderDetails failed", oError.message, "OrderController");
MessageBox.error(this.getText("errorLoadingOrder"));
}
}

 

8. Single Responsibility

One method does one thing. One class has one purpose.

  • If a method name contains "and", it is doing too much
  • If a method is longer than ~30–40 lines, question whether it should be split
  • AI must not generate monolithic functions that fetch, transform, and render all in one block
    ❌process_order_validate_and_send_email()
    ✅validate_order() + process_order() + notify_customer()

9. Testability

Code must be written in a way that allows it to be tested in isolation.

Rules:

  • Avoid tight coupling — dependencies should be injectable, not hardcoded
  • In ABAP, structure code to support ABAP Unit tests
  • In UI5, structure controllers to support QUnit tests
  • AI must flag when generated code is difficult to test and suggest how to refactor it

10 . Version & Dependency Awareness

  • Always specify which ABAP release, CDS/CAP version, or UI5 version the code targets
  • Do not use APIs or syntax that are deprecated or not yet available in the system landscape
  • If the system version is not known, ask before generating. Do not assume.

11. Don't Repeat Yourself (DRY)

If the same logic appears more than once, it belongs in a shared method, class, or utility.
AI must not copy-paste logic with minor variations — it must abstract it

12. Leave the Code Better Than You Found It

Apply the Boy Scout Rule: leave the campsite cleaner than you found it.

  • If you pass through code with an obvious issue (magic number, missing comment, deprecated method), fix it if safe — or leave a " TODO: note
  • This is not an invitation to refactor everything — scope it to what you touched
  • AI must flag improvement opportunities spotted during generation, without applying them unsolicited


13. Avoid over-engineering

Build what is needed now, but do not close doors for tomorrow. Avoid unnecessary complexity, but design with extensibility in mind. Hardcoded values, rigid structures, and tight coupling are not simplicity — they are technical debt.

  • AI must not introduce unnecessary abstraction layers, design patterns, or generic frameworks for simple problems
  • If a simpler solution exists, prefer it — even if a more complex one is technically "more correct"
  • Flag when a request itself may be over-scoped: "This could be solved more simply by..."

14. Say When You Are Not Sure

Honesty is a feature. If AI is uncertain about the correct approach, it must say so explicitly.
When uncertain, AI must:

  • State clearly: "I am not confident this is the correct approach for your version/context"
  • Suggest relevant SAP Community resources:
    SAP Community Blog
    SAP Help Portal
    SAP GitHub (CAP/UI5)
  • Never invent table names, function module names, or API endpoints — if unsure, flag it

15. Ask for more context if needed

AI must not make assumptions about the business context, system landscape, or intent.
When to ask before generating:

  • The system version is unknown (see Principle 10)
  • The business requirement is ambiguous
  • There are multiple valid approaches with different trade-offs
  • The scope of the change is unclear (one method? one class? one package?)
  • A few seconds asking the right question saves hours of rework.

16. Go Through the Front Door

SAP is not just a database — it is a business application with decades of logic, validations, and integrations built into its application layer. Writing directly to standard tables bypasses all of that. It corrupts data, breaks dependent processes, and creates problems that are silent at the time of the change and catastrophic later.

The rule is simple: if SAP provides a BAPI, function module, or API for an operation — use it. Always.

  • Never update, insert, or delete SAP standard tables directly. Standard SAP tables must never be modified with UPDATE, INSERT, MODIFY, or DELETE statements. Always use the BAPI, function module, or service provided by SAP for that operation.

" ❌ Never do this — bypasses all SAP business logic

UPDATE vbak SET gbstk = 'C' WHERE vbeln = lv_order_id.

" ✅ Use the correct BAPI

CALL FUNCTION 'BAPI_SALESORDER_CHANGE'
EXPORTING
salesdocument = lv_order_id


If no BAPI or API exists for a required operation, this must be escalated and documented before proceeding. It must never be solved with a direct table write without explicit approval.

  • Always check the RETURN table after every BAPI callBAPIs do not raise exceptions — they return errors, warnings, and success messages in a RETURN table. If you do not check it, errors pass silently and data may appear saved when it is not.
CALL FUNCTION 'BAPI_SALESORDER_CHANGE'
EXPORTING salesdocument = lv_order_id
TABLES return = lt_return.​

✅Always check for errors in the return table

READ TABLE lt_return
WITH KEY type = 'E'
TRANSPORTING NO FIELDS.

IF sy-subrc = 0.
" Error found — do not commit, handle it
RAISE EXCEPTION TYPE zcx_bapi_error.
ENDIF.
  • Always use COMMIT WORK after a successful BAPI call
    A BAPI call does not persist data on its own. You must explicitly commit the work unit. Equally, if an error is found in the RETURN table, always call ROLLBACK WORK to undo any partial changes.
    "✅ Commit only after confirming no errors
CALL FUNCTION 'BAPI_TRANSACTION_COMMIT'
EXPORTING wait = abap_true.​

" ✅ Rollback on error
CALL FUNCTION 'BAPI_TRANSACTION_ROLLBACK'.
Never use COMMIT WORK directly in BAPI-based flows — always use BAPI_TRANSACTION_COMMIT with WAIT = ABAP_TRUE to ensure the update task completes before proceeding.


⚠️This rule applies to classic ABAP and BAPI-based flows only. In RAP (Restful Application Programming), transaction handling is managed by the RAP framework. Never call COMMIT WORK or BAPI_TRANSACTION_COMMIT inside a RAP behaviour handler — the framework commits automatically after the save sequence completes successfully.


17. Deployment & Transport
This here changes from company to company. Consider documenting your transport lanes, approval gates, and naming conventions

18. Code Change Convention
All code changes must be wrapped with the following comment block, regardless of language.

*** <JIRA_TICKET_ID> - <Full Name> - <DD-MM-YYY> - Start
*** [Previous code or "N/A - New implementation"]
[New code here]
*** <JIRA_TICKET_ID> - <Full Name> - <DD-MM-YYY> - Finish


19. Inline Code Comments
When to Comment explain why, not what. The code should explain what it does. Comments explain decisions.

❌" Loop through orders (obvious)
✅" Filtering cancelled orders here because the OData service does not support this filter server-side

Your turn!

Do you use AI instructions with your team? What would you add to this list? What would you change or throw out?
