entry.title: SIT Porto 2026: A first time, and why I'll be back
entry.content:
Hello everyone, I'm Andrea. I've been working with SAP for over 20 years, across Brazil, Ireland and Portugal. And until this year, I had never heard of SIT or of a CodeJam, for that matter.

The DOM / Table of content of the post (nerdy joke in a technical blog, why not? 😂)

The DOM (Document Object Model) is how a browser sees a web page: a tree where every title, paragraph and image is a branch. Think of it as a map of the page. Here is the table of contents of this post, as a DOM.  

<post>
├──  1. So how did I find out about SIT
│ ├──  The hesitation about SIT
│ ├── The day before: another CodeJam
│ └── So, what is SIT?
├──  2. How SIT can matter for you and your career
│ ├── If you're new to SAP
│ ├── If you come from classic ABAP and you're on the move to the new world
│ └── If you're already an expert
├── 3. The investment
├── 4. The talks, and where to watch them
│ ├── Before we jump into the talks: A challenge!
│ ├── Where my notes will live
│ └── The talks
│ ├── At the venue
│ └── On the replay
└── 5. What's next

 

1. So how did I find out about SIT

A few months back, I was checking the community when I saw the post for the CodeJam Getting started with Generative AI Hub on SAP AI Core, happening in June 2026, and signed up. The event was already full, so I put my name down anyway, sure I wouldn't get in. A few days before the event, I got an email saying I was in. So I took a day off to go, bought a personal laptop the day before (yes, really), got bus tickets (the trains were already sold out) and went.  On the way back I had to run, literally until I couldn't run anymore, to catch my bus home.

All worth. The CodeJam was excellent. I saw a great value on it and that's how I started getting involved in SAP events in Portugal and becoming more active in the community.

The hesitation about SIT

So when SIT Porto came around, I hesitated. I was anxious about walking into a room full of deep experts in tools I'm still learning, not being able to keep up, or finding people who kept to their own bubbles. Maybe it was a bit of impostor syndrome talking very loudly (yes, even after 20 years). 

I went anyway. There were a few familiar faces from the CodeJams and one from my time in Brazil, and it was nice to see them again. And I was indeed surrounded by deep experts who kept it simple.

The atmosphere was incredibly welcoming: people at different career levels and with different levels of knowledge, all open to talking and exchanging ideas. And not just with their own colleagues, everyone was talking to everyone. The speakers stayed for the whole event, ready to chat and answer questions. It really was an event made for anyone in the SAP community, at any stage of their career.

The day before: another CodeJam

I also took part in the CodeJam AI-enabled integrations with SAP Integration Suite on September 25, at the same venue as SIT. But that's a story for another post 🙂 A tip for next year: check if there are other events scheduled around SIT.

So, what is SIT?

SIT is where people with fascinating topics get together to share their experience, and where everybody is open to new connections and to seeing the world "beyond their own box." It's a fantastic way to keep up to date and to extend your SAP network.

 

2. How SIT can matter for you and your career

If you're new to SAP

You will leave with a lot of new terms and technologies to learn. Also a lot of names that you can reaach out for help. Think of it as a map that you can then go deeper into. Watching demos of the newest SAP products at the start of your journey can shape your career.

If you come from classic ABAP and you're on the move to the new world

It's a chance to update your knowledge, and not only through the talks: the conversations show you where your peers are heading, what worked, what didn't, and the vocabulary of the moment. If you are really intentional about it, you can considerably extend your network.

If you're already an expert

Nobody is an expert in everything. SIT is a chance to sharpen what you know and to learn other sides of your bubble of knowledge. After 20+ years working with SAP, and a lot of studying of the new ecosystem, I left SIT (and every CodeJam, for that matter) with my head full of new terms, new tools and a long list of things to get deeper into.

3. The investment

One Saturday and €5. SIT happens every year around September, always on a Saturday, and this year's 3rd edition took place on September 26, 2026, at the Forte de Gaia hotel (Autograph Collection), right next to the postcard bridges of Porto. It is absolutely worth it.

More info: https://sitporto.com/

4. The talks, and where to watch them

Fátima Linhares, Business Unit Manager at Valantic , opened the day as our host and welcomed everyone.

The talks were varied, but all of them touched the same topic, and you won't believe which one: AI. Hahaha.

Before we jump into the talks: A challenge!

Before you jump to the summaries, I want to leave you with a challenge from António Andrade, who spoke about sovereignty: think about sovereignty in every talk. I accepted it, so at the end of each post I share my own take. I'd love to hear yours, so we can all grow by sharing ideas and find more ways to mature on this topic, which is so urgent today.

Where my notes will live

I love studying and learning, so I make notes on everything I learn about SAP. It's such a vast ecosystem, with so many concepts and tools, and it's so easy to forget things. So I'll be sharing my notes with you here. To stay updated, bookmark this post and leave a comment: I'll reply to it every time a new post goes live, so you'll know when it's out. And you're very welcome to follow me too!

A tip: today I use Obsidian to keep my notes. I love to see the Graph mode and how all things converge. Have you ever used it? Any other suggestions?

The talks

You can watch the whole event here: https://www.youtube.com/live/grU_TdxhjNY

At the venue
  1. The power of the SAP Community: Simplified Blogging and Personal Branding in the era of AI, Moshe Naveh (0:31). Staying authentic in the AI era is a real challenge. Moshe shares tips on getting more out of the SAP Community, and a simplified blogging workflow: template, recorded notes with transcript, a prompt to draft, then review, validate and publish. Watch it if you've always wanted to become more active in the community and build a personal brand in the SAP community.
  2. Sovereign Cloud in SAP: Innovation, Control and Trust in the Era of AI, António Andrade (1:00). Sovereignty broken into four layers (data, operational, technical and legal) and the options SAP presents: hyperscalers, SAP cloud infrastructure, sovereign cloud on-site and regional partners. Watch it if you're concerned about where your company's data is going and want to learn more about governance and sovereignty.
  3. From Sapphire Vision to the Autonomous Enterprise: What's Real, What's Next, Mustafa Bensan (1:36). Maps the Sapphire announcements onto the new SAP ecosystem, and shows how the startup LiveKit makes voice interaction with SAP possible. Watch it if Sapphire left you with puzzle pieces and no picture, and you want to see how the future sounds (pun intended) for SAP users.
  4. What's in Business Data Cloud today, and what will it be called tomorrow, Tim Koster (2:12). The evolution of SAP solutions into Business Data Cloud and SAP's data analytics strategy. Watch it if you've lost track of what everything is called, and want to know what's a real change to the tool and what's just a new fancy name.
  5. Event-driven architectures in the age of AI, António Maradiaga (2:46). Why event-driven architecture is reliable and how it works, with a real example from the previous day's CodeJam combining Joule, Integration Suite and MCP. Watch it if "event-driven" still sounds like a buzzword, and to see how the cool things work in the background.

Then we went to lunch, and I got to meet a lot of new people. I heard so many interesting views on how people are experiencing all these changes, and even learned where companies are right now and how they are handling this new era of autonomous enterprise and agentic AI.

Unfortunately I had to leave after lunch, because the train timetable in Portugal wasn't on my side (the train was 40 minutes late, and a trip that usually takes 1h took 4h30m 😒), so António Maradiaga's was the last talk I watched at the venue. I'm rewatching all of them on the replay to make my notes, which is why some summaries are still coming.

On the replay
  1. Autonomous Asset Management, Tiago Fernandes (5:10). Pairs with Mustafa's talk: the future of SAP is conversational, but Tiago argues agents change how we work without replacing people. Watch it if you've wondered what this means for our jobs and what the future might look like for companies.
  2. What Happens When You Give AI an SAP Data Migration Project? Paul Major (5:45). Real-world lessons from applying generative AI to an S/4HANA data migration. Coming soon.
  3. OriseX: From data to knowledge in just a few seconds, Afonso Ungaro. Coming soon.
  4. AI in SuccessFactors: From Copilot to document grounding, Hugo Ferreira. Coming soon.

5. What's next

I'm so excited for the next CodeJams and SITs!

More info: https://sitporto.com/

A note on how I write: I'm bilingual, so I mix languages when writing, because some things are funnier in one language than another 😂. I also use AI to help me translate it all and polish my posts, but the experiences, opinions and notes are mine.

entry.title: Accepting Payments in SAP Without Expanding Your PCI Footprint
entry.content:
Integrating payment acceptance into SAP can create significant efficiencies for Finance and A/R teams.

But it also raises an important question:

What happens to your PCI DSS scope when credit card payments become part of your SAP workflow?

Payment integration should simplify operations—not create unnecessary security and compliance responsibilities. That's one of the key advantages of processing payments through the SAP Digital Payments Add-On (DPA). By combining SAP's payment architecture with a certified PSP's payment processing capabilities, organizations can securely accept payments while limiting the exposure of sensitive cardholder data within their SAP environment.

Why PCI Scope Matters

The more systems, applications, and employees that interact with cardholder data, the more complicated securing that environment can become. Consider a traditional payment workflow. A customer provides card information to an employee, who enters it into a payment application. The transaction is processed separately and then reconciled back to SAP. Every additional touchpoint can introduce risk and potentially increase PCI compliance responsibilities. A better approach is to minimize where sensitive payment information exists in the first place.

Keeping Sensitive Card Data Out of SAP

One of the fundamental security components of the SAP Digital Payments Add-On is tokenization. Instead of storing the actual card number within SAP, sensitive payment information is handled within the secure payment-processing environment and replaced with a token. That token can then be used throughout the payment workflow without exposing the underlying card number within SAP.For Finance teams, payments remain connected to the SAP workflow. From a security perspective, however, sensitive cardholder data is kept away from the ERP environment.

The concept is simple:

If your systems don't need sensitive payment data, don't put it there.

This approach can help organizations:

  • Reduce exposure to sensitive cardholder data
  • Reduce the systems included within the PCI DSS environment
  • Limit unnecessary employee interaction with payment information
  • Reduce the risks associated with storing card data internally
  • Simplify ongoing security and compliance efforts

Reducing Human Exposure Matters Too

PCI scope isn't only about technology. Organizations should also consider how employees receive payment information. Are customers reading card numbers to A/R representatives over the phone? Is payment information being written down or sent through email? Are employees moving between SAP and another application to process transactions?

Each additional step creates another potential point of exposure. Integrated and tokenized payment workflows can reduce the number of employees and systems that need to interact with sensitive payment information. That's good security practice regardless of PCI requirements.

Security Without Sacrificing Efficiency

Improving security shouldn't make payment processing more difficult. Through the SAP Digital Payments Add-On, payment processing remains connected to the SAP workflow while the underlying payment credentials are handled securely outside the ERP. Finance teams can continue working within SAP while supporting payment authorization, settlement, tokenized payment credentials, cash application, reconciliation, and reporting.

For recurring customers, tokenization also means payment credentials can be securely referenced for future transactions without repeatedly collecting or exposing the underlying card information. The result is a more secure payment architecture without adding unnecessary friction to the Finance workflow.

Look Beyond the Transaction

When evaluating an SAP payment integration, organizations should look beyond whether the transaction can simply be processed.

Ask:

Where does the sensitive payment information go? Who can access it? Where is it stored? And how much of our environment becomes part of our PCI compliance responsibilities?

Those questions should be addressed as part of the integration strategy—not after implementation.

For Finance and IT teams, the objective is straightforward:

Integrate payments into SAP without unnecessarily expanding your payment-data footprint.

If your organization is evaluating payment acceptance within SAP, I'd welcome the opportunity to review your current payment workflow and identify areas where you may be able to improve security, reduce PCI scope, and simplify the overall payment process.

entry.title: New AI Features in SAP Enterprise Threat Detection, Cloud Edition
entry.content:
Security investigations are often complex and time-consuming. Monitoring agents must sift through vast amounts of log data, evaluate the risk posed by individual ABAP objects, and translate technical findings into clear, actionable recommendations.

Since August we've introduced three AI-assisted features in SAP Enterprise Threat Detection, cloud edition that help monitoring agents work more efficiently: Behavior analysis, criticality assessments for ABAP objects, and recommendation templates.

Let's take a closer look at what's new.

Behavior analysis: Let AI surface suspicious activity for you

When an investigation is underway and you've identified suspicious users through alerts, the harder question surfaces: what exactly did they do, and how serious was it? Manually reviewing large volumes of log data to answer that takes time you often don't have.

That's where behavior analysis comes in. From the Behavior Analysis tab on the investigation details page, you can trigger an AI-powered analysis of the users already linked to your investigation—without leaving your current context. The AI examines their activity across your event data and returns a list of suspicious log events, each tagged with a severity level (Very High, High, Medium, or Low) and an explanation of the AI's reasoning. You can then select individual events and assign them to your investigation as evidence.

 What you'll need: The UEBAManager role and accepted SAP AI Terms and Conditions

For more information, see Running a Behavior Analysis | SAP Help Portal.


Criticality information for ABAP objects: Know your risk at a glance

Not every ABAP object carries the same risk — but assessing that risk manually takes expertise and time. AI-assisted criticality assessments are now available for four ABAP object types: HTTP paths, function modules, transactions, and reports.

The assessment is available directly within the apps where you already work as a monitoring agent: Analyze Log Events, Manage Value Lists, Manage Investigations, and Manage Alerts. When you request criticality information for an object, the system returns:

  • A criticality level (Very High, High, Medium, Low, or Unknown)
  • A plain-language explanation of why the object is security-critical
  • Remediation recommendations to reduce the risk
  • Where applicable, details about relevant SAP Security Notes, including CVSS scores and publication dates

A feedback option lets you flag inaccurate or misleading AI-generated content helping improve results over time.

What you'll need: The roles CriticalObjectsAIManager and accepted SAP AI Terms and Conditions.

For more information, see Criticality Information for ABAP Objects | SAP Help Portal.

 

AI-assisted recommendation templates: Faster, more consistent investigation reports

When closing an investigation, monitoring agents write a recommendation for the customer — what happened, why it matters, and what to do next. Getting that right, consistently, across many different patterns, can be a challenge.

We've made it easier with AI-assisted recommendation templates. In the Manage Patterns app, you can now use a chat interface to describe the template you need, and the system generates a structured draft. You can then refine it through the chat or edit it directly before saving.

Each template follows a clear three-part structure: what happened (investigation result), why it matters (alert reason), and what to do (recommended action). Placeholders in the template are automatically filled with real event data when a monitoring agent generates a recommendation for a specific investigation.

You can create templates at two levels: global templates that apply across all tenants, and tenant-specific templates. SAP-provided templates for standard patterns are also available to view as a reference.

What you'll need: The roles CriticalObjectsAIManager and CrossTenantCriticalObjectsManager and accepted SAP AI Terms and Conditions.

For more information, see Creating Recommendation Templates | SAP Help Portal.

 

Wrapping up

These three features reflect a broader direction we're taking with SAP Enterprise Threat Detection: putting AI where it reduces friction in security work. Behavior analysis helps you focus on the activities that matter most. Criticality assessments give you instant context on risky ABAP objects without having to dig through documentation. And AI-assisted recommendation templates help you produce clearer, more consistent reports in less time.

Together, these innovations help security teams make better-informed decisions and respond faster to potential threats.

entry.title: What did our RBP model look like a year ago? Five practices for RBP governance in SAP SuccessFactors
entry.content:
Every SAP SuccessFactors implementation eventually reaches a point where questions about Role-Based Permissions (RBP) begin to surface from audit, compliance, security, or HRIS teams.

The questions are usually straightforward:

  • What changed?
  • Who approved it?
  • Why was the change made?

Behind those questions sits the one that often proves most difficult to answer:

What did our RBP model look like a year ago, and can we explain every change that has been made since then?

Most organizations can show what their permissions look like today. Far fewer can show what the permission model looked like six months ago, a year ago, or at the beginning of an audit period.

The reason is simple: if no historical snapshot was captured a year ago, then there is nothing to compare against later. Reconstructing that history often becomes a time-consuming exercise involving exported workbooks, email threads, approval records, change tickets, and whatever documentation survived the last release cycle.

The challenge is not simply understanding the current state. The challenge is maintaining a trustworthy record of what changed and who approved it.

What the Scale Actually Looks Like

To put this into perspective, one SAP SuccessFactors environment I analyzed contained approximately 90 permission roles, 200 grant rules, and 190 permission groups. Expanded out, those roles represented more than 110,000 individual permission entries.

At that scale, nobody identifies changes simply by reviewing screens or comparing exports manually.

In one comparison exercise, two snapshots differed by exactly two permissions out of more than 110,000. Two view permissions had been added to a role. Nothing in the standard administrative views made that obvious.

The same challenge exists with permission groups. A group's employee count might show a net increase of one when, in reality, three people were removed and four were added. A simple count would never reveal what actually changed.

A Simplified Example

Here is what answering an auditor's question looks like when historical records exist. This is a simplified example only meant to describe the process. 

  • January snapshot: The HR Business Partner role contains 412 permissions and is granted through an HRBP permission group.
  • April snapshot: The role now contains 413 permissions.
  • Difference identified: Compensation Information: View was added.
  • Reason for the change: A merit-cycle initiative required HR Business Partners to view compensation information.
  • Approval evidence: The change was approved by the appropriate business owner and documented in Change Ticket CHG-1042.
  • Audit outcome: Reviewers can see the before state, after state, the specific permission change, justification, approver, and supporting evidence.

Without the January snapshot, answering the same question may require searching through months of emails, tickets, and project documentation in the hope that someone preserved the information.

Five Practices That Improve RBP Governance

Whether you use spreadsheets, custom processes, governance tools, or other approaches, the organizations that manage RBP most effectively tend to follow several common practices.

1. Establish a Baseline

Capture a complete record of the permission model, including roles, permissions, permission group definitions, and grant rules.

One lesson I learned early on is that roles alone rarely tell the whole story. The grant rules often have as much governance significance as the permissions themselves because they determine who receives access and over whom that access applies.

A complete baseline provides a reference point for every future review.

To establish a baseline, organizations can use a variety of approaches, ranging from report downloads and API-based extracts to dedicated governance solutions that automate periodic captures and comparisons.

2. Capture on a Cadence That Matches Change Activity

Regular snapshots provide historical context. Additional captures around major releases, organizational restructures, quarterly access reviews, and implementation cutovers provide greater visibility during periods of significant change.

SAP SuccessFactors delivers major releases each year, and release-related configuration activities frequently introduce permission changes. Capturing snapshots before and after significant events can make it much easier to isolate and understand what changed.

The appropriate cadence varies by organization. Smaller environments may align captures with audit cycles or quarterly reviews, while larger and more complex environments may benefit from monthly captures.

3. Compare Changes at a Detailed Level

Knowing that a role changed is rarely enough. The valuable information is understanding exactly what changed, where the change occurred, and what the before-and-after values looked like.

In larger environments, comparisons can generate hundreds or even thousands of individual changes. Separating project-related modifications from routine operational updates helps reviewers focus on the changes that matter most.

Once the volume exceeds a few dozen changes, automated analysis becomes increasingly valuable.

4. Document the Business Justification

A list of changes is only part of the story. Governance improves significantly when each change is associated with a business justification, supporting evidence, and an accountable approver.

In practice, the approver is often not the same person who implemented the change, and the approval history may exist outside SAP SuccessFactors in emails, tickets, or project documentation.

Capturing that information when the review occurs is far easier than trying to reconstruct it months later.

5. Evaluate Segregation of Duties Regularly

Segregation of Duties (SoD) risks rarely appear all at once. More often, they emerge gradually as permissions are added, expanded, or combined across roles over time.

 
One observation from reviewing role structures is that unexpected risks often appear in small or temporary roles that gradually accumulate additional permissions over multiple projects and releases. As a result, SoD issues often go unnoticed until an audit uncovers them or an access-related issue occurs.

Including SoD in periodic review helps organizations identify potential conflicts before they surface during audits, access reviews, or compliance assessments.

Looking at RBP Through a Version-Control Lens

Over the years, I came to view RBP governance as a version-control problem. Thinking about it this way changed how I approached it.

If an organization cannot:

  • Show the state of the permission model at the start of an audit period
  • Explain what changed between two reviews
  • Identify who approved those changes and why

then audit preparation, access reviews, and compliance activities become significantly more difficult than they need to be.

Organizations that approach RBP governance using a structured, repeatable process are generally better positioned to support audits, simplify access reviews, and maintain confidence in their permission model over time.

I'd be interested in hearing how other SAP SuccessFactors teams approach RBP governance, change tracking, and audit readiness, particularly when answering the question:

"What did our RBP model look like a year ago?"

Share your experience in the comments.

entry.title: GRC Tuesdays: SAP GRC for SAP HANA What Happened Between Release and General Availability
entry.content:
When SAP GRC for SAP HANA 1.0 was released to customers on March 6, 2026, it marked an important milestone in the evolution of SAP Governance, Risk and Compliance solutions.

General Availability followed on July 31, 2026, opening the solution to a broader audience of customers and partners around the world. 

Source: SAP GRC for SAP HANA 1.0 in the SAP Product Availability Matrix

For readers looking for a detailed overview of the solution itself, its innovations and strategic direction, I recommend the SAP Community blog GRC Tuesdays: What’s New in SAP GRC for SAP HANA

However, a question has consistently surfaced since the release announcement. 

“So... what exactly happened during those five months?”

After all, software does not spend months sitting quietly in a digital waiting room.  

In reality, those months were packed with customer engagement, validation activities, feedback sessions and continuous improvements through SAP’s Early Adopter Care (EAC) program. 

The EAC program played a crucial role in ensuring that SAP GRC for SAP HANA was not only released, but truly ready for broader adoption. 

 

Putting SAP GRC for SAP HANA to the Test 

 

The purpose of the EAC program is straightforward. Rather than relying solely on internal testing, SAP works closely with selected customers and partners to validate software in real-world business environments. Participants implement, upgrade, test and evaluate the solution using their own processes, requirements and operational realities. 

For SAP GRC for SAP HANA, the EAC program brought together organizations from a diverse range of industries, including industrial manufacturing, software, technology, oil and gas, and life sciences. 

This variety was important. Every organization approaches governance, risk and compliance differently. By validating the solution across multiple industries and business scenarios, SAP was able to gain confidence that the solution delivers value beyond a single use case or deployment model. 

 

Real Projects, Real Scenarios 

 

Participants validated a broad range of capabilities across the SAP GRC portfolio. Solutions covered included SAP Access Control, Process Control, Risk Management, Audit Management and data protection capabilities.

Some organizations focused on system upgrades from existing SAP GRC environments. Others evaluated greenfield implementations. Several participants tested integration scenarios, operational processes and security requirements that reflected the complexity of modern enterprise landscapes. 

The importance of this cannot be overstated. Enterprise software succeeds when it works in the real world, not only in a controlled demonstration environment. The EAC program provided exactly that opportunity. 

 

The Results 

 

The outcome of the program was highly positive.

Participating organizations successfully completed their planned validation activities and finished the program with “Green” status. Customer feedback was strong, resulting in an average satisfaction score of 8.4 out of 10:

Equally important, issues identified during the program were quickly addressed and resolved, helping improve product quality, documentation and implementation guidance before broader market adoption. 

 

What Customers Appreciated Most 

 

Several themes consistently emerged from customer feedback

Performance improvements were frequently highlighted, particularly in business processes where responsiveness and reporting speed directly influence productivity. 

Participants also noted improvements in the user experience delivered through SAP Fiori-based interfaces. Simplified navigation and a more modern user interaction model were viewed positively by both business users and administrators. 

Reporting and analytics capabilities received strong marks as well. Customers appreciated enhanced visibility into governance, risk and compliance activities, helping them make more informed decisions and monitor their environments more effectively. 

Integration scenarios represented another success area. Participants successfully validated connectivity and identity-related scenarios while confirming that SAP GRC for SAP HANA can participate effectively within modern enterprise architectures. 

Finally, many participants highlighted the collaborative nature of the EAC program itself. Regular interaction with SAP product experts enabled rapid issue resolution and accelerated learning throughout implementations. Customers also appreciated ongoing documentation updates and greater roadmap transparency, which increased confidence in both the product direction and implementation journey.

 

Lessons Learned Along the Way 

 

The EAC program was not only about validating successes. It also generated valuable lessons that future customers can use to reduce project risk and accelerate their own transformations:

One important recommendation involves third-party software and add-ons. Customers found that compatibility assessments should begin early in the project lifecycle to avoid unexpected challenges later. 

Sandbox testing emerged as another major success factor. Organizations that invested time in comprehensive testing before moving forward experienced smoother project execution and fewer surprises during implementation. 

Integration validation also proved crucial. Testing interfaces, identity management configurations and connected processes early helped teams identify and resolve issues before they became business concerns. 

Documentation and planning were additional themes. As the EAC program progressed, implementation guidance continued to expand, helping future customers benefit from the experiences of those who participated first. 

The final lesson may be the most important. Success was consistently strongest where SAP, customers and partners worked closely together. Open communication and active collaboration accelerated outcomes for everyone involved. 

 

Looking Ahead 

 

The completion of the Early Adopter Care program represents more than the end of a validation cycle. It marks the beginning of broader customer adoption supported by real-world experience, practical implementation knowledge and proven success stories. 

The organizations that participated in the program helped shape the final release through testing, feedback and collaboration. Their contributions improved product quality, strengthened guidance and provided valuable insights for future adopters. 

For customers now assessing their next step, additional guidance is available in the SAP Community blog GRC Tuesdays: Why Move to SAP GRC for SAP HANA, which outlines business drivers and migration considerations. 

If you were wondering what happened between Release to Customer and General Availability, the answer is not 'not much'. It was five months of testing, collaboration, feedback and continuous improvement between customers, partners and SAP working together to ensure that SAP GRC for SAP HANA arrived not only as a new release, but as a solution validated by real organizations, solving real challenges and ready for real-world adoption.

And if you are interested in learning more about SAP solutions for Governance, Risk, and Compliance, feel free to fill-in the demo request form!

entry.title: The Unsung Hero of SAP GRC Access Control: Understanding Action Usage Synch
entry.content:
Every SAP GRC Access Control administrator has probably heard the phrases "transactional log" or "action usage data" thrown around in discussions. But how many people have actually stopped to think about where that data comes from, what makes it reliable, and what happens when the plumbing behind it quietly breaks? This post pulls back the curtain on the Action Usage Synch report — the background report that keeps GRC's action usage picture accurate — and explains why misconfiguring a single parameter can silently poison your compliance data for months.
 
What Is Action Usage Sync, and Who Uses the Data?
 
At its heart, Action Usage Synch (GRAC_ACTION_USAGE_SYNC) is a background report that bridges two worlds: the raw transaction logs living on your connected SAP systems (plugin systems), and the neatly structured GRC database tables that power reports, dashboards, and risk analysis. Every time a user executes a transaction code, initiates a WebDynpro application, consumes an OData service, or opens a Fiori Tile on a managed system, that execution is recorded in the system's performance statistics (STAD — System Transaction Analysis and Diagnosis), Gateway log, or Frontend statistics (FESR — FrontEnd Statistics Records). The Action Usage Sync job harvests those logs and translates them into two GRC-owned tables: 'GRACACTUSAGE', which stores individual execution events with full timestamps, user IDs, connectors, terminal info, and transaction codes; and 'GRACMGMTACTUSAGE', which maintains a rolled-up management view showing the execution count and last execution date per user-action-connector combination.
 
The consumers of this data are broader than most people realise. Role-level usage analysis in GRC Access Control relies on it — when you run a role usage report and see that a role's critical actions were "last used 14 months ago," that number comes from 'GRACMGMTACTUSAGE'. Risk owners who want to know whether a SoD-violating action combination was actually exercised, or just theoretically possible, look here. The Emergency Access Management module also has its own flavour of this mechanism: when a Firefighter User logs in via a Firefighter ID, the exact same GRACACTUSAGE data is eventually consolidated to the particular Firefighter Session by matching the timestamps. The connection between the Firefighter Session and the Action Usage data is stored in the 'GRACFFREPMAPP' table.
 
How It Works: A Journey Across Two Systems
 
The report runs on the GRC central system, but the actual transaction logs it needs are sitting on the connected managed (plugin) systems. This cross-system reach is what makes the architecture interesting.
 
When the job starts, it first resolves which connectors to process. It translates the user-provided connector range into a proper list of active connectors. Next, it determines the timestamp for each connector from which the sync should start. This information is stored in the 'GRACTASKEXECSTMP' table — a small but critical bookkeeping table that records the last successful execution timestamp per task per connector. The task key for this is 'ACTION_USAGE_SYNC'. This timestamp becomes the 'FROM' timestamp for the next run's log query, ensuring the job is always incremental and only asks for data that is genuinely new.
 
The actual data retrieval is where the RFC call happens. For SAP ABAP connectors — the typical case — the code resolves the RFC destination from the connector configuration, then calls a dedicated function module on the target system. This function module lives on the plugin component (GRCPINW, GRCPIBAS) and is responsible for reading STAD and — if enabled — OData Gateway and FESR logs there. The results — user name, transaction code, timestamp, terminal, program name, and a transaction ID — travel back to the main GRC system over RFC, which receives the data and maps it into the internal action log structure.
 
Back on the main GRC system, the report processes the returned records in batches. The 'Time Period' parameter (defaulting to 3,600 seconds, i.e. one hour) controls the size of each time slice sent to the RFC call. The total time range from the last execution timestamp to now is divided into chunks of that many seconds, and the RFC is called once per chunk. This prevents a single call from pulling an enormous payload after a long gap, and it also allows intermediate progress to be committed to the database between chunks. After processing each batch, the code persists individual records to 'GRACACTUSAGE' and upserts the aggregated execution counts in 'GRACMGMTACTUSAGE'. Alert action logs are also updated.
 
One deduplication mechanism deserves special mention: the 'GRACACTTRANS' table. This table stores connector–user ID–action–program ID–transaction ID tuples for recently seen transaction executions. Before inserting a new record from the RFC response, the code checks whether that particular action and program combination for the particular user has already been processed for the particular transaction. If it has, the record is skipped. After each successful run, 'GRACACTTRANS' is cleaned up: records older than the Retention Period in seconds (defaulting to 432,000 seconds — five days) are deleted. This sliding cleanup window is there purely to cap the table's growth while still protecting against duplicates across consecutive runs. The duplicate check is essential due to how STAD information is transformed into Action Usage information in GRC. Without this check, execution counts would not be accurate and the size of 'GRACACTUSAGE' would grow exponentially.
 
Parameters and Scheduling Frequency: Why Every Second Counts
 
The report exposes four parameters on its selection screen:
 
Connector: Restricts which connectors are processed. Leaving it empty processes all configured connectors. In large landscapes with many connectors, scoping this per connector and running parallel jobs staggered slightly in time can significantly improve throughput.
 
User: Restricts data collection for Firefighter Action Usage Synch to a specific set of users. This is relevant only in special cases when SAP Support instructs you to do so; for normal execution the value should always be completely empty.
 
Time Period: This is the parameter that most frequently causes operational grief. It defines the size of each RFC call's time slice in seconds. The default is 3,600 seconds (one hour), which serves a good balance between execution time and resource requirements. Decreasing the value means fewer resources are required (time and memory) to collect the action data per call; however, more RFC roundtrips will be required, and the overall execution time of the job will increase due to RFC overhead. Increasing the value means faster execution of the sync job, but significantly more resources will be required to collect the action data per call.
 
Retention Period: This parameter controls the retention period of the 'GRACACTTRANS' deduplication table, defaulting to 432,000 seconds (five days). Any data older than the configured time in seconds will be removed from 'GRACACTTRANS', and the duplicate check will no longer be able to detect it as a duplicate.
 
For the scheduling frequency, the answer depends on how current you need your action usage data to be. The standard recommendation is to run the job every hour. This ensures that the job collects all data created in the last hour, providing up-to-date information in your main GRC system. It also gives enough time to ensure that the action data is properly collected.
 
Running the job less frequently — say, daily — is not inherently wrong, but you will encounter longer execution times and you increase the risk of missing action information if you fail to detect that the job is not running properly. Because STAD data is stored for only 48 hours in the default configuration (for more information, check the profile parameter 'stat/max_files'), if you fail to collect the data within this timeframe, that data will be lost and can never be collected again.
 
Common Issue #1 — The User Field Is Filled When It Shouldn't Be
 
This one causes more confusion than you'd expect. When the Users parameter is populated, the report takes a completely different code path. Instead of collecting the normal action usage information, it executes a special process designed to collect data for Firefighter usage in emergency cases only. This is intentional design: populating the user field signals "I am syncing a specific Firefighter session," and GRC switches to the SPM connector infrastructure accordingly. In normal circumstances this is never required — this process is handled by the Firefighter Sync job — so you should only use it if specifically instructed to do so (mostly in cases where Action Usage Sync has never been executed because your business does not require that information, yet the Firefighter Log Sync job is not working for some reason).
 
The practical problem arises when an administrator — trying to narrow down a test run or debug a single user's data — enters a regular business user in the user field of the general Action Usage Sync job. The job will attempt to use the SPM connector path for a non-SPM user on a connector that may not have SPM configured at all. The run will collect information, but it will not register it in the Alert table and will not update the general Action Usage timestamp. The data collected in this mode is simply not regular Action Usage data, so you will not get accurate action-related information and metrics, and the root cause will not be immediately obvious.
 
The rule is simple: to run general Action Usage Synch, the user field should always be completely empty. Not even a whitespace or any wildcard character (* or ?) should be entered in this field. User-scoped runs are intended for emergency cases only and should be performed only when instructed by an expert.
 
Common Issue #2 — The Time Period Parameter Is Set Too Low or Too High
 
Too low: If Time Period is set to, say, 30 seconds, the report will issue 120 RFC calls to cover a single hour of data. This is technically functional but will hammer both the GRC system and the target system with rapid-fire RFC connections. Under heavy connector loads with many connectors, this can cause RFC work process saturation on the target. Worse, if each call takes more than a second or two due to STAD read overhead, the processing time for a single connector can stretch to minutes — blowing through the available batch window. This could increase the time required to finish the job, which could lead to consecutive scheduling issues. The safe lower bound is around 60 seconds (one minute) for systems with moderate usage volumes; however, if you need to set the value that low, it could indicate an improper resource configuration on your backend system. The optimal lower bound is 150–300 seconds.
 
Too high: The opposite extreme is setting the Time Period to a very large value — for instance, 86,400 seconds (one full day) — to "simplify" the chunking. The problem here is that a single RFC call now requests a full day's worth of STAD data in one go. STAD is not a small log source on busy production systems. Very large STAD reads can time out at the RFC layer, return with a communication failure, and leave the job's watermark timestamp un-updated. The next run will then attempt the same oversized time window again, fail again, and the data gap grows. If you observe frequent TSV_TNEW_PAGE_ALLOC_FAILED or TIME_OUT dumps in your connected backend system, that is a pretty good indication that the value is too high and you need to decrease it. This can occur even with the default value. In that case you should decrease the value and find the highest value at which dumps are no longer observed. STAD has an optimal read window of around 10 minutes, so setting the value somewhere between 300 and 600 seconds should work well in most cases.
 
Common Issue #3 — The Job Was Never Run, or Has Been Silent for a Long Time
 
This is the scenario that GRC teams tend to discover late — typically during an audit or a risk analysis review, when someone notices that action usage data for a critical system is either missing entirely or frozen at a date from twelve months ago.
 
When the 'GRACTASKEXECSTMP' entry for a connector does not exist (the job has never run), the report treats the start timestamp as empty, which the downstream code interprets as "start from the beginning of available data" — translated to the beginning of the UNIX epoch (19700101000000). In practice, this means the RFC call on the target system will attempt to retrieve the entire available STAD history — potentially weeks or months of transaction data — in chunks of the Time Period value each. This is the operational equivalent of asking someone to retype a library by hand. Even with an optimal Time Period value, an initial sync covering all data on an active system can take hours of continuous runtime and thousands of RFC calls. During this time the job holds RFC work processes on both systems and generates significant load. And — based on STAD retention — it will only actually find meaningful action data for the last 48 hours.
 
A similarly problematic situation arises when the job has been running but then stopped for an extended period — perhaps because the scheduled job variant was accidentally deleted, or the system connector was temporarily deactivated and then forgotten.
 
How to resolve it: There is a fully compliant but slow way, and there is a faster, more efficient option whose compliance depends on your policy.
 
The fully compliant way is to stop the currently scheduled Action Usage Synch (if it is running) and start it in ad-hoc mode with properly set parameters. Run the job until it finishes on its own, then restart it again in ad-hoc mode. Repeat this process until the job finishes within the required scheduling frequency, at which point you will be able to schedule it. The first few executions might take hours or even days depending on how long ago the last successful execution was, and the job will probably only collect data from the last 48 hours (or whatever the STAD retention value is set to on the backend system). Each iteration should complete more and more quickly, and eventually the job will finish within the desired scheduling window (SAP's recommendation is hourly execution). Using this method, you collect all available data and the job sets the appropriate timestamps and values (execution counts, last execution timestamps, etc.) as if it had been running throughout.
 
The faster option is to use the report GRAC_EAM_TASK_TIMESTAMP_UPDATE to set the last successful execution timestamp of the Action Usage Sync manually. Before doing this, first consult your compliance coordinator to confirm that this approach is acceptable under your policy. If it is, run the report in SA38/SE38, set the connector, enter the desired timestamp in the format YYYYMMDDHHMISS (for example, 13:45:00 on 26 April 2019 would be entered as 20190426134500), select "Action Usage Synch (All User)", and execute. This will set the timestamp in the 'GRACTASKEXECSTMP' table, after which you can run the job in the same ad-hoc manner described above — but it will complete significantly faster since it will not start from "the beginning."
 
For both the never-run case and the stale case, always check the GRC application log after the first successful run. Navigate to the log and filter by category 'ACT_SYNC' or program 'GRAC_ACTION_USAGE_SYNC', and verify that the run completed without RFC errors or return code failures. A successful run will log a confirming completion message for each connector. Any 'E'-type messages pointing to `Plugin connection returned with error` or `Connector not found` indicate that the connector infrastructure itself needs attention before the data sync can succeed.
 
Common Issue #4 — Missing Authorization Causes Missing Usernames
 
This is also a common issue that is frequently found and poses a significant problem: it cannot be repaired, and if you do not detect it early, your data can be corrupted for a long time. The sync job runs hourly, the Time Period parameter is set optimally, the job runs flawlessly and without errors — yet you do not see any action-related information in any GRC reports or screens. You see that the 'GRACACTUSAGE' and 'GRACMGMTACTUSAGE' tables are populated with data. Seemingly no error, no issue... so what went wrong? If you look at the 'GRACACTUSAGE' table closely, you can see one small clue. The User IDs look odd — as if someone replaced all the actual usernames with random gibberish characters. This is not a coincidence or a bug; it is a privacy configuration of STAD. STAD will conceal User IDs unless the user attempting to retrieve them — in our case the RFC connection user configured in SM59 for the configured connector — has the authorization object S_TOOLS_EX with the value S_TOOLS_EX_A for the AUTH field. This authorization is most likely missing from the RFC user on your connected backend system, which is why it cannot read the User IDs.
 
Common Issue #5 — Time Is of the Essence
 
The last common issue is incorrect timezone or timezone rule configuration across your backend system's OS, database, and SAP system configuration. All three must be configured to use the same timezone and the same timezone rule. This ensures that each system calculates the requested timestamps correctly. If any of them is misconfigured, data may not be read accurately and may not be returned to GRC correctly. To detect any misconfiguration, you can run report 'RSDBTIME' on both your main GRC system and your connected backend system. This can reveal any major misconfiguration. Correcting the values should resolve missing or improperly collected logs.
 
Closing Thoughts
 
Action Usage Synch is one of those jobs that is easy to underestimate because it does its work quietly in the background. When it runs correctly, it is invisible. When it breaks — wrong user filter, wrong time slice, wrong timezone, long-dormant watermark, missing authorization — the failure tends to be silent too: no alarms, no obvious dashboard warnings, just slowly staling compliance data waiting to embarrass you at the next audit cycle. Moreover, the data cannot be repaired; you will only have accurate data from the point at which you resolved the root cause.
 
Taking five minutes to understand its parameters, scheduling it at a sane frequency, and periodically verifying its application logs is a small investment for a large return. The data it produces powers some of GRC's most valuable risk reduction capabilities. Treat the scheduler like the compliance instrument it is.
